Layered Monoidal Theories II: Fibrational Semantics
Leo Lobski, Fabio Zanasi

Abstract
Layered monoidal theories provide a categorical framework for studying scientific theories at different levels of abstraction, via string diagrammatic algebra. We introduce models for three closely related classes of layered monoidal theories: fibrational , opfibrational and deflational theories. We prove soundness and completeness of these theories for the respective models. Our work reveals connections between layered monoidal theories and well-known categorical structures such as Grothendieck fibrations and displayed categories.

1
Introduction

Layered monoidal theories generalise
monoidal
theories: their diagrammatic language allows several monoidal theories to be combined, together with functorial translations between them, all within a single string diagram. The motivation for the formalism is that a single system may admit multiple intertranslatable descriptions at different levels of granularity. Examples include chemical reactions, which may be modelled abstractly as reaction networks or more finely as molecular graphs
2
, and computer architecture, where high-level descriptions must ultimately be implemented as microelectronic circuits
17
. In Part I of this work
19
, we focussed on the
syntax
of layered monoidal theories. In this second part, we introduce their
semantic models
and investigate questions of soundness and completeness. Since we begin by recalling the syntax, the exposition is self-contained.

A layered monoidal theory consists of several monoidal theories, together with monoidal functors between them. A typical term in a layered theory is drawn on the left of Figure
1
, where
x
is a term in the monoidal theory
\omega
(drawn as a box on the left) and
y
is a term in the monoidal theory
\tau
(drawn as a box on the right). The dotted lines indicate that
x
and
y
sit above
\omega
and
\tau
, and that the “functor boundary”
\blacktriangleleft_{f}
sits above
f
. Terms may slide through the functor boundaries from one monoidal theory to another, as shown on the right of Figure
1
. Albeit highly intuitive, this is a purely syntactic formalism, leaving open how to semantically interpret such structures. In this paper we show that these diagrammatic transformations can be interpreted in a sound way in well-studied mathematical structures. Beyond establishing internal coherence of the formalism, our work reveals a connection between layered monoidal theories and well-known categorical structures, such as fibrations
10
;
4
;
12
;
14
;
20
and displayed categories
1
;
3
.

As a necessary step towards semantics, we need to refine the classification of layered monoidal theories. The definition of a layered monoidal theory (Definition
3.13
) requires specifying a
recursive sorting procedure
(Definition
3.5
), which determines what kinds of terms are available within the theory. The role of such terms is to control what kinds of translations are present
between
the layers -- as opposed to the usual monoidal terms within a single layer. Different recursive sorting procedures give rise to different theories, even if the signature is kept fixed
1
1

1

Note that this is a departure from how monoidal theories are usually developed: in that case, there is a single sorting procedure, and consequently just one class of models – (strict) monoidal categories.
. We shall consider three different (but related) recursive sorting procedures, corresponding to three classes of models. Namely, we define
opfibrational
,
fibrational
and
deflational
theories. The first two serve as building blocks for the third, which is the most expressive and central to our development.

The distinction between opfibrational, fibrational and deflational theories can be understood in terms of the functor boundaries (labelled as
\blacktriangleleft_{f}
in Figure
1
). The choice of the direction of the functor boundary is, in principle, arbitrary: one may write
\omega
on the right and
\tau
on the left, while still depicting the functorial translation
f:\omega\rightarrow\tau
. It is, therefore, desirable to have a formalism where both directions are present, and the interaction between the functor boundaries is axiomatised. While the equations governing the behaviour of the boundaries should be symmetric, it is
a priori
not clear how to obtain both directions simultaneously.
In deflational theories, the most expressive case, boundaries indeed come in two forms: each generator between layers gives rise to both a “forward” and a “backward” boundary.

Opfibrational theories only contain the left-to-right functor boundaries as in Figure
1
, while fibrational theories reverse this direction. The two are mirror images of one another in all respects, and their corresponding models are categorically dual. Deflational theories are obtained by “glueing” the fibrational and the opfibrational version of the same theory along their shared internal morphisms (denoted by
x
and
y
in Figure
1
), thereby producing bidirectional boundaries. As a consequence of the modular construction of the theories, we need three classes of models – one for each kind of theory mentioned above:
opfibrations with indexed monoids
,
fibrations with indexed comonoids
and
monoidal deflations
are the models of opfibrational, fibrational and deflational theories, respectively.

The paper establishes three soundness and completeness results, each arising from a free-forgetful adjunction. We summarise the results in Table
1
: the first column lists the relevant theory, while the second column indicates the semantic structures with respect to which it is sound and complete. We include the classical result for monoidal theories as a point of reference. As expected from the close connection between the theories, the semantic structures are tightly linked: each (split) opfibration with indexed monoids contains models for monoidal theories as its fibres; each (split) fibration with indexed comonoids is obtained by dualising a (split) opfibration with indexed monoids; and the 1-categorical part of a (split) monoidal deflation is obtained by glueing a (split) opfibration with indexed monoids with its dual (split) fibration with indexed comonoids

From another perspective, (op)fibrational layered theories provide a string diagrammatic language for (strict)
indexed monoidal categories
. Moeller and Vasilakopoulou introduced a
monoidal Grothendieck construction

23
, which provides an equivalence between (op)indexed monoidal categories and pseudomonoids in the category of (op)fibrations. The present work can be seen as the first step towards a diagrammatic treatment of this result. However, we remark that, unlike in
23
, all the monoidal categories that we treat as models are
strict
; see Subsection
2.4
.

In light of their connection to indexed monoidal categories, one might reasonably call the theories under study
indexed monoidal
rather than
layered monoidal
. However, indexed monoidal categories provide a proper subclass of models of layered monoidal theories – an important class that is not contained in indexed monoidal theories are deflations (Section
5
). We therefore retain the term layered to emphasise the broader scope of the framework.

Structure of the article.

We begin by covering quite some background in Section
2
. After briefly defining terms and equations for layered theories in Section
3
, we introduce
opfibrations with indexed monoids
in Section
4
and
monoidal deflations
in Section
5
. These will, respectively, provide the models for the
opfibrational
and
deflational
layered theories. Section
6
contains the main results of the article: we show that terms organise themselves into
free models
upon quotienting by appropriate structural equations.

2
Preliminaries

Here we cover the preliminaries needed to follow the ensuing discussion, and give references to the relevant literature for more details. While most things are more or less known, we use this section to establish some notational and terminological conventions that will be used throughout the paper. Specifically, we cover (op)fibrations
2.1
, retrofunctors
2.2
, indexed categories
2.3
, profunctors
2.5
, profunctor collages
2.6
and monoidal theories
2.7
.

2.1
Fibrations and opfibrations

While (op)fibrations were originally introduced by Grothendieck
10
, here we mostly follow Jacobs
12
. Other expository texts include Borceux
4
, Johnstone
14
and Loregian & Riehl
20
.

A functor is usually denoted by a lowercase Latin letter
p:\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow\mathcal{X}
, or just by an arrow
\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow\mathcal{X}
with no symbol.

Given a functor
p:\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow\mathcal{X}
, we say that an object
y\in\mathcal{O}b(\mathcal{Y})
is
above
an object
x\in\mathcal{O}b(\mathcal{X})
if
py=x
. Similarly, a morphism
g\in\mathcal{Y}
is above a morphism
f\in\mathcal{X}
if
pg=f
. Given a morphism
f\in\mathcal{X}
, we denote by
\mathcal{Y}_{f}
the set of all morphisms above
f
. In the special case when
f
is an identity on some object
x\in\mathcal{O}b(\mathcal{X})
, this defines the subcategory of
\mathcal{Y}
known as the
fibre
of
x
: the objects are all objects of
\mathcal{Y}
above
x
, the morphisms are all morphisms above
\mathsf{id}_{x}
. We denote the fibre of
x
simply by
\mathcal{Y}_{x}
.

Given a function
p:\mathcal{O}b(\mathcal{Y})\rightarrow\mathcal{O}b(\mathcal{X})
, a
liftable pair

(f:x\rightarrow y,b)
consists of a morphism
f\in\mathcal{X}
and an object
b\in\mathcal{O}b(\mathcal{Y})
with
pb=y
. Similarly, an
opliftable pair

(a,f:x\rightarrow y)
consists of a morphism
f\in\mathcal{X}
and an object
a\in\mathcal{O}b(\mathcal{Y})
with
pa=x
.

Let us fix a functor
p:\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow\mathcal{X}
.

Definition 2.1

(Opcartesian map)
.

A morphism
F:a\rightarrow b
in
\mathcal{Y}
is called
p
-opcartesian
if for any morphism
G:a\rightarrow c
in
\mathcal{Y}
and any morphism
h:pb\rightarrow pc
in
\mathcal{X}
such that
pF;h=pG
(i.e. the lower triangle below commutes), there is a unique morphism
H:b\rightarrow c
above
h
such that
F;H=G
(i.e. the upper triangle below commutes):

Remark 2.2

(Weakly opcartesian map)
.

We obtain the notion of a
weakly
p
-opcartesian map
upon restricting the quantification to
h
being the identity map in the above definition: for any morphism
G:a\rightarrow c

with
pc=pb
such that
pF=pG
, there is a unique map
H
above
\mathsf{id}_{pb}
with
F;H=G
. Clearly, each opcartesian map is, in particular, weakly opcartesian. The converse does not hold in general.

Definition 2.3

(Opfibration)
.

A functor
p:\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow\mathcal{X}
is an
opfibration
if for every opliftable pair
(a,f:x\rightarrow y)
, there is a
p
-opcartesian morphism
F:a\rightarrow b
above
f
:

}.

Such morphism
F
is called an
opcartesian lifting
of
(a,f:x\rightarrow y)
. Note that we drop the prefix
p
if the functor is clear from the context.

In the context of (op)fibrations, we refer to the domain category
\mathcal{Y}
as the
total
category, and to the codomain category
\mathcal{X}
as the
base
category.

Remark 2.4

(Preopfibration)
.

We obtain the notion of a
preopfibration
if we require
F
in the above definition to be
weakly

p
-opcartesian rather than
p
-opcartesian.

By the defining universal property of opcartesian maps, opcartesian liftings are unique up to an isomorphism. An opfibration which comes with a choice of an opcartesian lifting for each opliftable pair is called
cloven
.

If
p:\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow\mathcal{X}
is a cloven opfibration, then every morphism
f:x\rightarrow y
in
\mathcal{X}
induces a functor between the fibres
f^{*}:\mathcal{Y}_{x}\rightarrow\mathcal{Y}_{y}
by mapping each
a\in\mathcal{Y}_{x}
to the codomain of the chosen opcartesian lifting of
(a,f:x\rightarrow y)
, and each morphism
G\in\mathcal{Y}_{x}
to the unique map above
\mathsf{id}_{y}
induced by the universal property of the opcartesian lifting of the liftable pair
(\mathtt{dom}(G),f)
, where
\mathtt{dom}(G)
is the domain of
G
. The functor
f^{*}
is referred to as the
reindexing functor
induced by
f
. In fact, defining a reindexing functor for each morphism in the base category of an opfibration is equivalent to providing a choice of opcartesian liftings.

Proposition 2.5
.

Any cloven opfibration
p:\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow\mathcal{X}
induces a pseudofunctor
\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathbf{Cat}
by sending each object to its fibre and each morphism
f
to the functor
f^{*}
.

We say that an opfibration is
split
if the induced pseudofunctor is, in fact, a functor: i.e. if for all
x\in\mathcal{O}b(\mathcal{X})
, the induced functor
\mathsf{id}_{x}^{*}
is the identity functor on
\mathcal{Y}_{x}
and for all composable maps we have
(f;g)^{*}=f^{*};g^{*}
.

Remark 2.6
.

Note that the construction of the reindexing functor
f^{*}:\mathcal{Y}_{x}\rightarrow\mathcal{Y}_{y}
already works for a preopfibration. However, the resulting assignment is not compositional (not even up to an isomorphism): the composition of two weakly opcartesian maps need not be weakly opcartesian. Thus, Proposition
2.5
fails for a preopfibration: its proof relies on the liftings being opcartesian (rather than merely weakly opcartesian). However, a preopfibration does induce a normal lax functor
\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathbf{Prof}
into the 2-category of profunctors. We return to this in Section
2.6
(see specifically Proposition
2.33
).

A fibration is the dual notion to opfibration, hence all the discussion here also holds for fibrations – with the directions appropriately reversed.

Definition 2.7

(Fibration)
.

Given a functor
p:\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow\mathcal{X}
, a morphism
F:a\rightarrow b
in
\mathcal{Y}
is
p
-cartesian
if it is
p
-opcartesian for
p:\mathcal{Y}^{op}\rightarrow\mathcal{X}^{op}
. The functor
p:\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow\mathcal{X}
is a fibration if
p:\mathcal{Y}^{op}\rightarrow\mathcal{X}^{op}
is an opfibration.

The intuition behind (op)fibrations is that they capture indexing via disjoint unions of indexed sets. We demonstrate this with the following example.

Example 2.8

(Family fibration)
.

Define the category
\mathtt{Fam}(\mathbf{Set})
of
families of sets
as follows:

•

the objects are pairs
(I,f)
of a set
I
and a function
f:I\rightarrow\mathbf{Set}
assigning to each element
i\in I
a set
f(i)
,

•

a morphism
(I,f)\rightarrow(J,g)
is a pair
\left(u,\left\{u_{i}\right\}_{i\in I}\right)
of a function
u:I\rightarrow J
and a family of functions
u_{i}:f(i)\rightarrow g(u(i))
,

•

the identity on
(I,f)
is given by
(\mathsf{id}_{I},\mathsf{id}_{fi})
,

•

the composition of
(u,u_{i}):(I,f)\rightarrow(J,g)
and
(v,v_{j}):(J,g)\rightarrow(K,h)
is given by
(u;v,u_{i};v_{ui})
.

The projection
\mathtt{Fam}(\mathbf{Set})\rightarrow\mathbf{Set}
to the first component is a fibration:

•

the cartesian maps
(u,\mathsf{id}_{fi}):(I,f)\rightarrow(J,g)
are given by commutative triangles

I
J
\mathbf{Set}
u
f
g

and the family of identity maps on each set
f(i)=g(u(i))
,

•

given a family of sets
(I,f)
and a function
u:J\rightarrow I
, the cartesian lifting is given by

\left(u,\mathsf{id}_{(u;f)(j)}\right):(J,u;f)\rightarrow(I,f).

Note that in Example
2.8
, we did not use the structure of
\mathbf{Set}
in the second component as the target of the indexing, apart from the fact that it is a category. This example, therefore, generalises to an arbitrary category: the category of
families over
\mathcal{C}
is denoted by
\mathtt{Fam}(\mathcal{C})
, and the projection to the first component
\mathtt{Fam}(\mathcal{C})\rightarrow\mathbf{Set}
is still a fibration.

Fibrations and opfibrations organise into categories. We will mostly focus on the fixed base case, however, the general case will also appear occasionally.

Definition 2.9

(Morphism of (op)fibrations)
.

Let
p
and
q
in the diagram below be (op)fibrations. A
morphism

(H,K):p\rightarrow q
is a pair of functors such that the square

\mathcal{Y}
\mathcal{X}
p
\mathcal{Z}
\mathcal{W}
q
H
K

commutes, and
H
sends
p
-(op)cartesian maps to
q
-(op)cartesian maps.

We denote the resulting categories of fibrations and opfibrations by
\mathbf{Fib}
and
\mathbf{OpFib}
. For a fixed base category
\mathcal{X}
, there are also categories of (op)fibrations into
\mathcal{X}
, whose morphisms are commutative triangles which preserve the (op)cartesian maps: this is a special case of a morphism defined above when the functor
K
between the bases is the identity. We denote the fixed base categories by
\mathbf{Fib}(\mathcal{X})
and
\mathbf{OpFib}(\mathcal{X})
.

Given a morphism of (op)fibrations
(H,K):p\rightarrow q
, observe that
H
sends
p
-(op)cartesian liftings to
q
-(op)cartesian liftings of the image of the (op)liftable pair under
K
. In the case of cloven (and hence split) opfibrations, we additionally require that the chosen liftings are preserved. The subcategories of split (op)fibrations are denoted by adding a subscript
\mathsf{sp}
in all four cases defined above: the objects are split (op)fibrations, while morphisms are morphisms of (op)fibrations such that chosen liftings are mapped to chosen liftings.

Two important properties of (op)fibrations are closure under composition and pullbacks. We record this in the following propositions.

Proposition 2.10
.

If
p:\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow\mathcal{X}
and
q:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{Z}
are (op)fibrations, then
p;q:\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow\mathcal{Z}
is also an (op)fibration.

Proposition 2.11
.

Let
p
in the diagram below be an (op)fibration. If the square

\mathcal{W}
\mathcal{Z}
p
\mathcal{Y}
\mathcal{X}
q

is a pullback, then
q
is also an (op)fibration.

The above propositions imply that the categories
\mathbf{Fib}(\mathcal{X})
and
\mathbf{OpFib}(\mathcal{X})
are cartesian, with the cartesian products given by pullbacks. The terminal object is given by the identity functor
\mathsf{id}_{\mathcal{X}}:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{X}
. We denote the resulting cartesian categories by
(\mathbf{Fib}(\mathcal{X}),\boxtimes,\mathsf{id}_{\mathcal{X}})
and
(\mathbf{OpFib}(X),\boxtimes,\mathsf{id}_{\mathcal{X}})
.

2.2
Retrofunctors

A split opfibration may be thought of as a way of providing chosen liftings for a functor in a way that is (1) functorial (it strictly preserves identities and composition), (2) compatible with the functor in the sense that the lifting is above the morphism that induces it, and (3) minimal in the sense made precise by the requirement of being opcartesian (Definition
2.1
). If we drop the third requirement (minimality), we obtain the notion of a
lens
, which provides
some
functorial assignment of liftings compatible with the functor. Further, dropping the second condition (compatibility), we obtain the notion of a
retrofunctor
, which is simply a functorial assignment of lifts. Note that this does not require any functor to be present in order to be defined – a function on object suffices. We remark that retrofunctors are more commonly known in the literature as
cofunctors
. However, we agree with Di Meglio
8
that the term cofunctor is misleading, as the concept is not dual to a functor in any meaningful way. We therefore stick to
retrofunctor
. We follow Clarke
5
in our definition of a retrofunctor.

Definition 2.12

(Retrofunctor)
.

A
retrofunctor

(p,\varphi):\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow\mathcal{X}
consists of a function
p:\mathcal{O}b(\mathcal{Y})\rightarrow\mathcal{O}b(\mathcal{X})
and a function
\varphi
from the opliftable pairs to
\mathcal{M}or(\mathcal{Y})
satisfying the following properties:

•

the opliftable pair
(a,f:x\rightarrow y)
is mapped to
\varphi(a,f):a\rightarrow a^{\varphi}
, where the codomain
a^{\varphi}
is above
y
, i.e.
p\left(a^{\varphi}\right)=y
,

•

\varphi(a,\mathsf{id}_{pa})=\mathsf{id}_{a}
, and
\varphi(a,f;g)=\varphi(a,f);\varphi\left(a^{\varphi},g\right)
.

We depict the action of a retrofunctor as follows:

2.3
Indexed categories

We define indexed and opindexed categories, and state the well-known equivalence between (op)fibrations and (op)indexed categories.

Definition 2.13

((Op)indexed category)
.

An
\mathcal{X}
-opindexed category
is a pseudofunctor
I:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathbf{Cat}
. Dually, an
\mathcal{X}
-indexed category
is a pseudofunctor
I:\mathcal{X}^{op}\rightarrow\mathbf{Cat}
.

We write the natural isomorphisms that witness the pseudofunctor structure as
c_{f,g}:I(f;g)\xrightarrow{\sim}I(f);I(g)
and
u_{x}:I(\mathsf{id}_{x})\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathsf{id}_{Ix}
.

We say that an (op)indexed category is
strict
when the pseudofunctor is an actual functor.

Given a small category
\mathcal{X}
, we denote the categories of
\mathcal{X}
-indexed and
\mathcal{X}
-opindexed categories by
\mathbf{ICat}(\mathcal{X})
and
\mathbf{OpICat}(\mathcal{X})
, whose morphisms are given by pseudonatural transformations. The strict versions are denoted by adding the subscript
\mathsf{st}
, where the morphisms are ordinary natural transformations.

Definition 2.14

(Grothendieck construction)
.

Given a pseudofunctor
I:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathbf{Cat}
, the
Grothendieck construction
is the category
{Gr}(\mathcal{X})
defined as follows:

•

objects are pairs
(x,a)
, where
x\in\mathcal{O}b(X)
and
a\in\mathcal{O}b(Iy)
,

•

morphisms
(f,F):(x,a)\rightarrow(y,b)
are pairs of a morphism
f:x\rightarrow y
in
\mathcal{X}
and a morphism
F:(If)(a)\rightarrow b
in
I(y)
,

•

the identity on
(x,a)
is given by
(\mathsf{id}_{x},(u_{x})_{a})
,

•

the composite of
(f,F):(x,a)\rightarrow(y,b)
and
(g,G):(y,b)\rightarrow(z,c)
is given by

\left(f;g,(c_{f,g})_{a};(Ig)(F);G\right).

The following equivalence is well-known. We give a proof sketch, and suggest the reader who has not seen the details before to complete the proof, as it is instructive, and all of the subsequent developments will build on this equivalence.

Theorem 2.15
.

Let
\mathcal{X}
be a small category. There are equivalences of categories

\displaystyle\mathbf{Fib}(\mathcal{X})

\displaystyle\simeq\mathbf{ICat}(\mathcal{X})

\displaystyle\mathbf{OpFib}(\mathcal{X})

\displaystyle\simeq\mathbf{OpICat}(\mathcal{X}).

Moreover, the equivalences restrict to split (op)fibrations and strict (op)indexed categories:

\displaystyle\mathbf{Fib}_{\mathsf{sp}}(\mathcal{X})

\displaystyle\simeq\mathbf{ICat}_{\mathsf{st}}(\mathcal{X})

\displaystyle\mathbf{OpFib}_{\mathsf{sp}}(\mathcal{X})

\displaystyle\simeq\mathbf{OpICat}_{\mathsf{st}}(\mathcal{X}).

Proof sketch.

The left-to-right functor sends each (op)fibration to the pseudofunctor defined in Proposition
2.5
. The right-to-left functor sends each
\mathcal{X}
-(op)indexed category to the projection
{Gr}(\mathcal{X})\rightarrow\mathcal{X}
to the first component from the Grothendieck construction.
∎

In fact, the above equivalences extend to 2-equivalences of 2-categories by adding the appropriate 2-cells to all the categories: we will, however, focus on the 1-categorical case here.

2.4
(Op)fibrations with pseudomonoids and indexed monoidal categories

Moeller and Vasilakopoulou
23
have extended the equivalence between (op)fibrations and (op)indexed categories in Theorem
2.15
to include monoidal structure. In fact, they have extended it in two ways: in the first case, each fibre is equipped with monoidal structure, which is preserved by the morphisms between the fibres; in the second case, there is a monoidal structure on the total and the base categories, which is preserved by the (op)fibration. Following Shulman
27
, we refer to the first (‘fiberwise’) case as
internal
monoidal structure, while to the second (‘global’) case as
external
monoidal structure. The two cases are, in general, distinct: we refer the reader to
23
for the details. Here we briefly sketch the situation of the first case, as our theory will build on a special case thereof.

On the side of (op)fibrations, the monoidal structure is captured by a pseudomonoid in the cartesian categories
(\mathbf{Fib}(\mathcal{X}),\boxtimes,\mathsf{id}_{\mathcal{X}})
and
(\mathbf{OpFib}(X),\boxtimes,\mathsf{id}_{\mathcal{X}})
. A pseudomonoid in one of these categories is given by a triple
(\mathcal{Y},\otimes,\mathbf{1})
, where
\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow\mathcal{X}
is an object (i.e. an (op)fibration), while
\otimes:\mathcal{Y}\boxtimes\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow\mathcal{Y}
and
\mathbf{1}:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{Y}
are morphisms, i.e. the diagrams

\mathcal{Y}
\mathcal{Y}\boxtimes\mathcal{Y}
\otimes
\mathcal{X}
\mathcal{Y}
\mathcal{X}
\mathbf{1}
\mathcal{X}
\mathsf{id}_{\mathcal{X}}

commute, and each functor preserves (op)cartesian maps, such that the usual unitality and associativity equations hold up to natural isomorphisms. A morphism of pseudomonoids is given by a morphism of (op)fibrations which commutes with the multiplication and the unit, again up to a natural isomorphism. We denote the resulting categories of pseudomonoids by
\mathbf{PsMonFib}(\mathcal{X})
and
\mathbf{PsMonOpFib}(\mathcal{X})
. If the pseudomonoids are required to be actual monoids strictly preserved by the morphisms, the resulting categories of monoids are denoted by
\mathbf{MonFib}(\mathcal{X})
and
\mathbf{MonOpFib}(\mathcal{X})
.

On the side of (op)indexed categories, the monoidal structure is captured by requiring the image of the pseudofunctor into
\mathbf{Cat}
to be, in fact, contained in
\mathbf{MonCat}
.

Definition 2.16

((Op)indexed monoidal category)
.

An
\mathcal{X}
-opindexed monoidal category
is a pseudofunctor
I:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathbf{MonCat}
. Dually, an
\mathcal{X}
-indexed monoidal category
is a pseudofunctor
I:\mathcal{X}^{op}\rightarrow\mathbf{MonCat}
.

We say that an (op)indexed monoidal category is
strict
if the pseudofunctor is an actual functor and its image is contained in
\mathbf{MonCat}_{\mathsf{st}}
, that is, each monoidal category and functor are strict.

Similarly to the plain indexed case, we denote the resulting categories by
\mathbf{IMonCat}(\mathcal{X})
and
\mathbf{OpIMonCat}(\mathcal{X})
, and add the subscript
\mathsf{st}
in the strict case.

Warning 2.17
.

The terms “indexed monoidal category” and “monoidal indexed category” are not used consistently in the literature. Some authors use it to refer to the external case when the indexing category
\mathcal{X}
itself has a monoidal structure, and the pseudofunctor is required to preserve it in some sense. The terminology of Definition
2.16
is consistent with Hofstra & De Marchi
11
and Ponto & Shulman
25
.

The following extends Theorem
2.15
to (op)fibrations with pseudomonoids and (op)indexed monoidal categories.

Theorem 2.18

(Moeller and Vasilakopoulou
23
, Theorem 3.14)
.

Let
\mathcal{X}
be a small category. There are equivalences of categories

\displaystyle\mathbf{PsMonFib}(\mathcal{X})

\displaystyle\simeq\mathbf{IMonCat}(\mathcal{X})

\displaystyle\mathbf{PsMonOpFib}(\mathcal{X})

\displaystyle\simeq\mathbf{OpIMonCat}(\mathcal{X}).

As for Theorem
2.15
, this is, in fact, part of a 2-equivalence between 2-categories upon adding the appropriate 2-cells to all the categories.

While it would be interesting to study graphical languages for the general (non-strict) case as presented above, this would take us too far from the currently existing string diagrams for monoidal categories, almost all of which are only understood well in the strict case. Here, we therefore focus on the strict case stated below, and leave studying the non-strict case using the methods developed here for future work.

Theorem 2.19
.

Let
\mathcal{X}
be a small category. There are equivalences of categories

\displaystyle\mathbf{MonFib}_{\mathsf{sp}}(\mathcal{X})

\displaystyle\simeq\mathbf{IMonCat}_{\mathsf{st}}(\mathcal{X})

\displaystyle\mathbf{MonOpFib}_{\mathsf{sp}}(\mathcal{X})

\displaystyle\simeq\mathbf{OpIMonCat}_{\mathsf{st}}(\mathcal{X}).

Proof.

Let
(\mathcal{Y},\otimes,\mathbf{1})
be a monoid on a split opfibration
\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow\mathcal{X}
. For each
x\in\mathcal{O}b(\mathcal{X})
, this defines a functor

\displaystyle\otimes_{x}:\mathcal{Y}_{x}\times\mathcal{Y}_{x}

\displaystyle\rightarrow\mathcal{Y}_{x}

\displaystyle(a,b)

\displaystyle\mapsto a\otimes b,

and the unit is given by
\mathbf{1}(x)\in\mathcal{O}b(\mathcal{Y}_{x})
. Associativity and unitality follow from those of
\otimes
and
\mathbf{1}
.

Conversely, given a functor
\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathbf{MonCat}_{\mathsf{st}}
(i.e. a strict opindexed monoidal category), we define the monoid on the Grothendieck construction as follows:

(\otimes_{x},I_{x})
denotes the monoidal structure in the category indexed by
x\in\mathcal{O}b(\mathcal{X})
. Associativity and unitality now follow from the corresponding properties of strict monoidal categories. Moreover, the triangles above commute by definition, and opcartesian maps (i.e. pairs whose second component is the identity) are preserved by strictness of the monoidal structure.

2.5
Profunctors

We follow Loregian
21
in our discussion of profunctors. We fix the convention that profunctors are contravariant in the first variable, and covariant in the second one. Profunctors are also known under the names of
distributors
,
relators
,
correspondences
and
bimodules
.

Definition 2.20

(Profunctor)
.

Let
\mathcal{A}
and
\mathcal{B}
be small categories. A
profunctor
from
\mathcal{A}
to
\mathcal{B}
is a functor
\mathcal{A}^{op}\times\mathcal{B}\rightarrow\mathbf{Set}
.

We denote a profunctor
P
from
\mathcal{A}
to
\mathcal{B}
by
P:\mathcal{A}\mathbin{\relbar\joinrel\negmedspace\mapstochar\joinrel\negmedspace\rightarrow}\mathcal{B}
. Thus, a profunctor assigns to each objects
a\in\mathcal{O}b(\mathcal{A})
and
b\in\mathcal{O}b(\mathcal{B})
a set
P(a,b)
, which we think of as “morphisms”
a\rightsquigarrow b
between objects in different categories
3
3

3

Such arrows are sometimes called
proarrows
or
heteromorphisms
.
. The action of
P
on morphisms is contravariant in the first variable (morphisms of
\mathcal{A}
) and covariant in the second variable (morphisms of
\mathcal{B}
):

}.

The assignment is functorial:
P(\mathsf{id}_{a},\mathsf{id}_{b})
is the identity function on the set
P(a,b)
, and
P(f^{\prime};f,g;g^{\prime})=P(f,g);P(f^{\prime},g^{\prime})
. These assumption ensure that the arrows
a\rightsquigarrow b
behave essentially like morphisms within a category, which leads one to ask how to compose two such arrows. This leads to defining composition of two profunctors.

Given profunctors
P:\mathcal{A}\mathbin{\relbar\joinrel\negmedspace\mapstochar\joinrel\negmedspace\rightarrow}\mathcal{B}
and
Q:\mathcal{B}\mathbin{\relbar\joinrel\negmedspace\mapstochar\joinrel\negmedspace\rightarrow}\mathcal{C}
, their composite profunctor
P;Q:\mathcal{A}\mathbin{\relbar\joinrel\negmedspace\mapstochar\joinrel\negmedspace\rightarrow}\mathcal{C}
is defined on objects by the following coend formula

P;Q(a,c)\coloneq\int^{b\in\mathcal{B}}P(a,b)\times Q(b,c)\coloneq\left.\raisebox{1.00006pt}{$\coprod\limits_{b\in\mathcal{B}}P(a,b)\times Q(b,c)$}\middle/\raisebox{-1.00006pt}{$\sim$}\right.,

(2.21)

where
\sim
is the equivalence relation on the set
\coprod_{b\in\mathcal{B}}P(a,b)\times Q(b,c)
generated by requiring that for all
f\in P(a,b)
,
g\in\mathcal{B}(b,b^{\prime})
and
h\in Q(b^{\prime},c)
one has

\left(f,Q(g,\mathsf{id}_{c})(h)\right)\sim\left(P(\mathsf{id}_{a},g)(f),h\right).

}.

(2.22)

Note that the equivalence relation defined above can be thought of as a kind of associativity condition, ensuring that the situation

a
b
b^{\prime}
c
f
g
h

unambiguously defines an element in
P;Q(a,c)
. In the next section, we shall see a construction making this formal: the above arrows will become actual morphisms within the same category, and the equivalence relation will guarantee associativity. We do not discuss the general theory of coends here, and simply treat the expression on the right-hand side of (
2.21
) as the definition of the coend on the left. For a detailed exposition, we refer the reader to Loregian
21
.

Example 2.23
.

Let
\mathcal{A}
be a category. Then the assignment

\displaystyle\mathcal{A}^{op}\times\mathcal{A}

\displaystyle\rightarrow\mathbf{Set}

\displaystyle(a,b)

\displaystyle\mapsto\mathcal{A}(a,b)

\displaystyle\left(f:a^{\prime}\rightarrow a,g:b\rightarrow b^{\prime}\right)

\displaystyle\mapsto f;{-};g:A(a,b)\rightarrow A(a^{\prime},b^{\prime})\ ::\ h\mapsto f;h;g

defines a profunctor
\mathcal{A}\mathbin{\relbar\joinrel\negmedspace\mapstochar\joinrel\negmedspace\rightarrow}\mathcal{A}
.

Definition 2.24
.

The
bicategory of profunctors

\mathbf{Prof}
has

•

all small categories as the 0-cells,

•

all profunctors as the 1-cells,

•

given profunctors
P,Q:\mathcal{A}\mathbin{\relbar\joinrel\negmedspace\mapstochar\joinrel\negmedspace\rightarrow}\mathcal{B}
, the 2-cells
P\rightarrow Q
are given by the natural transformations,

•

the composition
\mathbf{Prof}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})\times\mathbf{Prof}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C})\rightarrow\mathbf{Prof}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{C})
is given by (
2.21
) and (
2.22
),

•

the identity on a 0-cell
\mathcal{A}
is given by the profunctor in Example
2.23
,

•

composition and identities for 2-cells are those for the natural transformations.

There are two ways to embed
\mathbf{Cat}
into
\mathbf{Prof}
: both embedding functors are identity on objects, one is contravariant on the 2-cells, while the other is contravariant on the 1-cells. Hence, let us denote by
\mathbf{Cat}^{co}
the category with the same 0- and 1-cells as in
\mathbf{Cat}
, and whose 2-cells are those of
\mathbf{Cat}
with the direction reversed. Similarly, let us denote by
\mathbf{Cat}^{op}
the category with the same 0- and 2-cells as in
\mathbf{Cat}
, but whose 1-cells are reversed.

First, let us define

-^{\blacktriangleleft}:\mathbf{Cat}^{co}\rightarrow\mathbf{Prof}

by mapping the functor
F:\mathcal{A}\rightarrow\mathcal{B}
to the following profunctor:

\displaystyle F^{\blacktriangleleft}:\mathcal{A}^{op}\times\mathcal{B}

\displaystyle\rightarrow\mathbf{Set}

\displaystyle(a,b)

\displaystyle\mapsto\mathcal{B}(Fa,b)

\displaystyle\left(f:a^{\prime}\rightarrow a,g:b\rightarrow b^{\prime}\right)

\displaystyle\mapsto Ff;{-};g:B(Fa,b)\rightarrow B(Fa^{\prime},b^{\prime})\ ::\ h\mapsto Ff;h;g,

and by mapping a natural transformation
\eta:F\rightarrow G
to the natural transformation
\eta^{\blacktriangleleft}:G^{\blacktriangleleft}\rightarrow F^{\blacktriangleleft}
whose
(a,b)
-component is given by
\eta_{a};{-}
.

Likewise, we define

-^{\vartriangleright}:\mathbf{Cat}^{op}\rightarrow\mathbf{Prof}

by mapping the functor
F:\mathcal{A}\rightarrow\mathcal{B}
to the following profunctor:

\displaystyle F^{\vartriangleright}:\mathcal{B}^{op}\times\mathcal{A}

\displaystyle\rightarrow\mathbf{Set}

\displaystyle(b,a)

\displaystyle\mapsto\mathcal{B}(b,Fa)

\displaystyle\left(f:b^{\prime}\rightarrow b,g:a\rightarrow a^{\prime}\right)

\displaystyle\mapsto f;{-};Fg:B(b,Fa)\rightarrow B(b^{\prime},Fa^{\prime})\ ::\ h\mapsto f;h;Fg,

and by mapping a natural transformation
\eta:F\rightarrow G
to the natural transformation
\eta^{\vartriangleright}:F^{\vartriangleright}\rightarrow G^{\vartriangleright}
whose
(b,a)
-component is given by
{-};\eta_{a}
.

Proposition 2.25
.

Let
F:\mathcal{A}\rightarrow\mathcal{B}
be a functor (i.e. a 1-cell in
\mathbf{Cat}
). Then the 1-cells
F^{\blacktriangleleft}
and
F^{\vartriangleright}
are adjoint with

F^{\blacktriangleleft}\dashv F^{\vartriangleright}

in the bicategory
\mathbf{Prof}
.

Proof.

The unit 2-cell
\eta:\mathsf{id}_{\mathcal{A}}\rightarrow F^{\blacktriangleleft};F^{\vartriangleright}
is defined as

\displaystyle\eta_{a,a^{\prime}}:\mathcal{A}(a,a^{\prime})

\displaystyle\rightarrow\int^{b\in\mathcal{B}}\mathcal{B}(Fa,b)\times\mathcal{B}(b,Fa^{\prime})

\displaystyle f

\displaystyle\mapsto(Ff,\mathsf{id}_{Fa^{\prime}}),

while the counit 2-cell
\varepsilon:F^{\vartriangleright};F^{\blacktriangleleft}\rightarrow\mathsf{id}_{\mathcal{B}}
is defined as

\displaystyle\varepsilon_{b,b^{\prime}}:\int^{a\in\mathcal{A}}\mathcal{B}(b,Fa)\times\mathcal{B}(Fa,b^{\prime})

\displaystyle\rightarrow\mathcal{B}(b,b^{\prime})

\displaystyle(g,h)

\displaystyle\mapsto g;h.

Naturality and the triangle equations now follow by observing that for the composite
F^{\blacktriangleleft};F^{\vartriangleright}
we have
(f,g)\sim(\mathsf{id}_{Fa},f;g)
for all
f\in\mathcal{B}(Fa,b)
and
g\in\mathcal{B}(b,Fa^{\prime})
, and similarly, for the composite
F^{\vartriangleright};F^{\blacktriangleleft}
we have
(Ff,g)\sim(\mathsf{id}_{Fa},Ff;g)
for all
f\in\mathcal{A}(a,a^{\prime})
and
g\in\mathcal{B}(Fa^{\prime},b)
.
∎

Remark 2.26
.

We observe that the counit 2-cell defined in the proof of Proposition
2.25
has surjective components on the image of the functor
F
. More precisely, for all
a,a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}
, the function

\varepsilon_{Fa,Fa^{\prime}}:\int^{a^{\prime\prime}\in\mathcal{A}}\mathcal{B}(Fa,Fa^{\prime\prime})\times\mathcal{B}(Fa^{\prime\prime},Fa^{\prime})\rightarrow\mathcal{B}(Fa,Fa^{\prime})

is surjective: a section is given by mapping
h:Fa\rightarrow Fa^{\prime}
to
(\mathsf{id}_{Fa},h)
. The surjectivity of the components will allow us to introduce the sections for the counit 2-cells for deflational theories in Subsection
3.1
.

2.6
Collages

The notion of a
collage
generalises the Grothendieck construction (see Section
2.3
) from (op)fibrations to arbitrary functors. What one gets on the other side of the equivalence are
displayed categories
, and a functor is obtained from a displayed category by taking its collage.

The term
displayed category
was introduced by Ahrens and Lumsdaine
1
for the purposes of studying fibrations in the type theoretic setting, where equivalence of their presentation with the notion used in Definition
2.27
is pointed out. The definition used here, as well as Theorem
2.29
and Proposition
2.32
are discussed in the notes taken by Streicher based on Bénabou’s course
3
.

Let
\mathcal{X}
and
\mathcal{Y}
be bicategories. Recall that a
lax functor

(D,\varphi):\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{Y}
consists of:

•

a function
D:\mathcal{O}b(\mathcal{X})\rightarrow\mathcal{O}b(\mathcal{Y})
,

•

for all
x,y\in\mathcal{X}
, a functor
D:\mathcal{X}(x,y)\rightarrow\mathcal{Y}(Dx,Dy)
,

•

for all
x\in\mathcal{X}
, a 2-cell
\varphi^{x}:\mathsf{id}_{Dx}\rightarrow D(\mathsf{id}_{x})
in
\mathcal{Y}
,

•

for all composable morphisms
f:x\rightarrow y
and
g:y\rightarrow z
in
\mathcal{X}
, a 2-cell
\varphi^{f,g}:D(f);D(g)\rightarrow D(f;g)
in
\mathcal{Y}
which is natural in
f
and
g
,

such that lax associativity and unitality diagrams commute (see e.g.
18
;
13
). We refer to the natural collections of 2-cells
\varphi
as the
laxators
. We say that a lax functor is
normal
if for each
x\in\mathcal{O}b(\mathcal{X})
, the laxator
\varphi^{x}
is the identity, i.e.
\mathsf{id}_{Dx}=D(\mathsf{id}_{x})
.

Definition 2.27

(Displayed category)
.

Let
\mathcal{X}
be a small 1-category. A
displayed category
is a normal lax functor
(D,\varphi):\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathbf{Prof}
.

Every functor
p:\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow\mathcal{X}
induces a displayed category
D_{p}:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathbf{Prof}
as follows:

•

for every
x\in\mathcal{O}b(\mathcal{X})
, let
D_{p}(x)\coloneq\mathcal{Y}_{x}
,

•

for every morphism
f:x\rightarrow y
in
\mathcal{X}
, define

given

, the laxator
\varphi_{p}^{f,g}:D_{p}(f);D_{p}(g)\rightarrow D_{p}(f;g)
is defined componentwise for each
a\in\mathcal{Y}_{x}
and
c\in\mathcal{Y}_{z}
by

\displaystyle\left(\varphi_{p}^{f,g}\right)_{a,c}:\int^{b\in\mathcal{Y}_{y}}D_{p}(f)(a,b)\times D_{p}(g)(b,c)

\displaystyle\rightarrow D_{p}(f;g)(a,c)

\displaystyle(F,G)

\displaystyle\mapsto(F;G).

Note that the lax functor so defined is indeed normal:
D_{p}(\mathsf{id}_{x})=\mathcal{Y}_{x}(-,-)=\mathsf{id}_{D_{p}(x)}
.

Definition 2.28

(Collage)
.

Given a displayed category
(D,\varphi):\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathbf{Prof}
, its
collage
is the category
\coprod D
defined as follows:

•

the objects are pairs
(x,a)
, where
x\in\mathcal{X}
and
a\in D(x)
,

•

a morphism
(f,F):(x,a)\rightarrow(y,b)
consists of a morphism
f:x\rightarrow y
in
\mathcal{X}
and an element
F\in D(f)(a,b)
,

•

the identity on
(x,a)
is given by
(\mathsf{id}_{x},\mathsf{id}_{a})
,

•

the composition of
(f,F):(x,a)\rightarrow(y,b)
and
(g,G):(y,b)\rightarrow(z,c)
is given by
\left(f;g,\varphi^{f,g}_{a,c}(F,G)\right)
.

Note that there is a forgetful functor
\coprod D\rightarrow\mathcal{X}
projecting the objects and the morphisms to their first component. The key observation by Bénabou is that
any
functor into
\mathcal{X}
arises as the collage of some displayed category. In order to state this result, let us define the category
\mathbf{Disp}(\mathcal{X})
as having all displayed categories
\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathbf{Prof}
as objects, and the morphisms are all lax transformations whose components are in the image of the embedding
-^{\blacktriangleleft}:\mathbf{Cat}^{co}\rightarrow\mathbf{Prof}
.

Theorem 2.29

(Bénabou)
.

Let
\mathcal{X}
be a small category. The slice category over
\mathcal{X}
is equivalent to the category of displayed categories on
\mathcal{X}
:

\left.\raisebox{1.02228pt}{$\mathbf{Cat}$}\middle/\raisebox{-1.02228pt}{$\mathcal{X}$}\right.\simeq\mathbf{Disp}(\mathcal{X}).

Proof sketch.

Given a functor
p
into
\mathcal{X}
, the corresponding displayed category is given by
D_{p}
. Conversely, given a displayed category
D
on
\mathcal{X}
, the corresponding functor is given by the projection from the collage
\coprod D
into
\mathcal{X}

∎

We refer the reader to
3
,
28
and
(
21
, Theorem 5.4.5)
for the detailed discussion and proofs.

Collage of a displayed category, together with Theorem
2.29
allow to detect properties of displayed categories on
\mathcal{X}
via properties of functors into
\mathcal{X}
. We shall need two such properties, namely, we characterise when
D:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathbf{Prof}
is a pseudofunctor (rather than merely a lax functor) and when it factors through
\mathbf{Cat}
. In the latter case, each morphism in
\mathcal{X}
is, in fact, indexing a functor, so that we have an indexed category
\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathbf{Cat}
, showing that displayed categories generalise indexed categories, while the collage is indeed a generalised Grothendieck construction.

Definition
2.30
characterises those functors which correspond to pseudofunctorial displayed categories. In order to state the definition, we need the notion of
path components
above a pair of composable maps, which we now proceed to describe.

Given a functor
\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow\mathcal{X}
, a pair of composable maps
f:x\rightarrow y
and
g:y\rightarrow z
in
\mathcal{X}
and objects
a\in\mathcal{Y}_{x}
and
c\in\mathcal{Y}_{z}
in the fibres over
x
and
z
, let us define the category
\mathcal{Y}(f,g)(a,c)
as follows:

•

the objects
(F,b,G)
are composable pairs
F:a\rightarrow b
and
G:b\rightarrow c
such that
b\in\mathcal{Y}_{y}
,
F
is above
f
and
G
is above
g
,

•

a morphism
H:(F,b,G)\rightarrow(F^{\prime},b^{\prime},G^{\prime})
is a map
H:b\rightarrow b^{\prime}
in the fibre
\mathcal{Y}_{y}
such that the diagram below commutes:

}.

We say that two objects in
\mathcal{Y}(f,g)(a,c)
are in the same
path component
if they are related by the equivalence relation generated by stipulating that
(F,b,G)\sim(F^{\prime},b^{\prime},G^{\prime})
if there is a morphism
(F,b,G)\rightarrow(F^{\prime},b^{\prime},G^{\prime})
. In other words, two composable pairs are in the same path component if there is a zigzag of morphisms between them.

Definition 2.30

(Factorisation lifting)
.

We say that a functor
\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow\mathcal{X}
is a
factorisation lifting
if for any morphism
F:a\rightarrow c
in
\mathcal{Y}
above
f:x\rightarrow z
, whenever there are morphisms
g:x\rightarrow y
and
g^{\prime}:y\rightarrow z
such that
g;g^{\prime}=F
, there are induced morphisms
G:a\rightarrow b
and
G^{\prime}:b\rightarrow c
above
G
and
G^{\prime}
, respectively, such that
G;G^{\prime}=F
:

Remark 2.31
.

What we call a
factorisation lifting
is usually called a
Conduché fibration
, a
Conduché functor
or an
exponentiable functor
. However, we consider the term
factorisation lifting
more suggestive of the property such functor is required to satisfy. The term
exponentiable
should be reserved to the property of the last bullet point of Proposition
2.32
. Said proposition then establishes that a functor is a factorisation lifting if and only if it is exponentiable.

By analogy with (op)fibrations, a factorisation lifting is
cloven
if it comes with chosen lifts for each factorisation. Further, a cloven factorisation lifting is
split
if the composition of any chosen lifts is the chosen lift of the composition, and the chosen lift of the trivial factorisation (either
f;\mathsf{id}_{z}
or
\mathsf{id}_{x};f
) is the corresponding trivial factorisation (
F;\mathsf{id}_{c}
or
\mathsf{id}_{a};F
).

The following proposition is due to Giraud
9
and Conduché
6
. A detailed discussion can be found in Street
28
.

Proposition 2.32
.

For any functor
p:\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow\mathcal{X}
, the following are equivalent:

•

p
is a factorisation lifting,

•

the displayed category
D_{p}:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathbf{Prof}
is a pseudofunctor,

•

the functor
p^{*}:\left.\raisebox{1.02228pt}{$\mathbf{Cat}$}\middle/\raisebox{-1.02228pt}{$\mathcal{X}$}\right.\rightarrow\left.\raisebox{1.02228pt}{$\mathbf{Cat}$}\middle/\raisebox{-1.02228pt}{$\mathcal{Y}$}\right.
defined by taking pullbacks has a right adjoint.

We only prove the equivalence of first two bullet points, as this suffices for developing the subsequent theory. The third one is stated for the sake of completeness of the presentation: the reader is referred to Street
28
for the proof.

Proof.

Observe that the laxator of
D_{p}

\left(\varphi_{p}^{f,g}\right)_{a,c}:\int^{b\in\mathcal{Y}_{y}}D_{p}(f)(a,b)\times D_{p}(g)(b,c)\rightarrow D_{p}(f;g)(a,c)

is an isomorphism if and only if for all
H:a\rightarrow c
above
f;g
there are
F:a\rightarrow b
and
G:b\rightarrow c
above
f
and
g
such that
F;G=H
, and such pair is unique up to the equivalence defining the coend, i.e. precisely when
p
is a factorisation lifting.
∎

In light of Proposition
2.32
, a factorisation lifting being cloven corresponds to a choice of an inverse for each component of the laxator of
D_{p}
. If such choice of inverses is, moreover, functorial in both
f
and
g
, the factorisation lifting is split.

The following proposition and the ensuing corollary connect our discussion of displayed categories and collages to opfibrations.

Proposition 2.33
.

A functor
p:\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow\mathcal{X}
is an preopfibration if and only if the displayed category
D_{p}:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathbf{Prof}
factors through the embedding
-^{\blacktriangleleft}:\mathbf{Cat}^{co}\rightarrow\mathbf{Prof}
.

Proof.

Observe that we have a natural isomorphism

D_{p}(f)(a,b)
\mathcal{Y}_{y}(Fa,b)
D_{p}(f)(a^{\prime},b^{\prime})
\mathcal{Y}_{y}(Fa^{\prime},b^{\prime})
\sim
\alpha_{a,b}
\sim
\alpha_{a^{\prime},b^{\prime}}
A;-;B
F(A);-;B

for some functor
F:\mathcal{Y}_{x}\rightarrow\mathcal{Y}_{y}
if and only if the opliftable pair
(a,f:x\rightarrow y)
has a weak opcartesian lifting
f_{a}:a\rightarrow F(a)
for each
a\in\mathcal{Y}_{x}
. To prove this, we argue as follows. If such liftings exist, then
F\coloneq f^{*}
is the usual reindexing functor between the fibres, and the isomorphism is given by the universal property of weak opcartesian maps: any
F^{\prime}:a\rightarrow b
in
D_{p}(f)(a,b)
uniquely factorises as

(a,f:x\rightarrow y)
as
\alpha^{-1}_{a,Fa}\left(\mathsf{id}_{Fa}\right)

∎

Corollary 2.34
.

For a preopfibration
\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow\mathcal{X}
, the following are equivalent:

•

it is an opfibration,

•

it is a factorisation lifting,

•

the composition of weakly opcartesian maps is weakly opcartesian.

Proposition
2.33
and Corollary
2.34
, of course, dualise to (pre)fibrations. Namely, a functor
p:\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow\mathcal{X}
is an prefibration if and only if the displayed category
D_{p}:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathbf{Prof}
factors through the embedding
-^{\vartriangleright}:\mathbf{Cat}^{op}\rightarrow\mathbf{Prof}
, and Corollary
2.34
holds verbatim upon removing ‘op’ throughout.

2.7
Monoidal theories and models

The terms for monoidal theories, upon quotienting by the structural identities
2.38
, give rise to
string diagrams

15
;
16
;
26
;
24
, which are sound and complete with respect to monoidal categories.

Definition 2.35

(Monoidal signature)
.

A
monoidal signature
is a pair
(C,\Sigma)
of a set
C
and a function
\Sigma:C^{*}\times C^{*}\rightarrow\mathbf{Set}
.

Given a monoidal signature
(C,\Sigma)
, the elements of
C
are called
colours
, and for
a,b\in C^{*}
, the elements in
\Sigma(a,b)
are the
monoidal generators
with arity
a
and coarity
b
.

A
morphism
between two monoidal signatures
\left(f,f_{a,b}\right):(C,\Sigma)\rightarrow(D,\Gamma)
consists of a function
f:C\rightarrow D
, and for each pair
(a,b)\in C^{*}\times C^{*}
, a function
f_{a,b}:\Sigma(a,b)\rightarrow\Gamma\left(f^{*}a,f^{*}b\right)
. We denote the resulting category of monoidal signatures by
\mathbf{MSgn}
.

Definition 2.36

(Terms of a monoidal signature)
.

Given a monoidal signature
(C,\Sigma)
, the set of
sorts
is given by
C^{*}\times C^{*}
. The
terms
are generated by the recursive sorting procedure below:

When using the linear notation, we denote the terms generated by the above rules by
\sigma
,
\mathsf{id}_{a}
,
\mathsf{id}_{\varepsilon}
,
(t;s)
and
(t\otimes s)
, respectively. We denote the set of terms by
\texttt{Term}_{C,\Sigma}
, and by
S:\texttt{Term}_{C,\Sigma}\rightarrow C^{*}\times C^{*}
the “underlying sort function" mapping
t:(a,b)\mapsto(a,b)
.

A pair of terms
(t,s)\in\texttt{Term}_{C,\Sigma}\times\texttt{Term}_{C,\Sigma}
is
parallel
if
S(t)=S(s)
. Let us denote the set of parallel terms by
P_{C,\Sigma}
.

Given a morphism
f:(C,\Sigma)\rightarrow(D,\Gamma)
of monoidal signatures, it immediately extends to a function on terms, also denoted by
f:\texttt{Term}_{C,\Sigma}\rightarrow\texttt{Term}_{D,\Gamma}
, by recursively defining:

\sigma:(a,b)\mapsto f_{a,b}(\sigma):(f^{*}a,f^{*}b)
,

\mathsf{id}_{a}:(a,a)\mapsto\mathsf{id}_{fa}:(fa,fa)
,

\mathsf{id}_{\varepsilon}:(\varepsilon,\varepsilon)\mapsto\mathsf{id}_{\varepsilon}:(\varepsilon,\varepsilon)
,

(t;s):(a,c)\mapsto\left(f(t);f(s)\right):(f^{*}a,f^{*}c)
,

(t\otimes s):(ac,bd)\mapsto\left(f(t)\otimes f(s)\right):(f^{*}(ac),f^{*}(bd))
.

Observe that
f:\texttt{Term}_{C,\Sigma}\rightarrow\texttt{Term}_{D,\Gamma}
preserves parallel terms: if
(t,s)\in P_{C,\Sigma}
, then
(ft,fs)\in P_{D,\Gamma}
.

Definition 2.37

(Monoidal theory)
.

A
monoidal theory

\mathcal{T}
is a triple
(C,\Sigma,E)
, where
(C,\Sigma)
is a monoidal signature, and
E\subseteq P_{C,\Sigma}
is a set of parallel terms. We refer to
E
as the
equations
of
\mathcal{T}
.

A morphism of monoidal theories
f:(C,\Sigma,E)\rightarrow(D,\Gamma,F)
is given by a morphism of monoidal signatures
f:(C,\Sigma)\rightarrow(D,\Gamma)
such that for all
(s,t)\in E
, we have
(fs,ft)\in F
. We denote the category of monoidal theories by
\mathbf{MTh}
.

Definition 2.38

(Structural identities)
.

Given a monoidal signature
(C,\Sigma)
, the set of
structural identities

S
is given by the following equations, where
s
,
s_{i}
and
t_{i}
range over the terms of the appropriate type:

Definition 2.39

(Term congruence)
.

Given a monoidal theory
(C,\Sigma,E)
, the
term congruence

\overset{E}{=}
is the smallest equivalence relation on
\texttt{Term}_{C,\Sigma}
generated by
E\cup S
, which is a congruence with respect to
;
and
\otimes
, i.e. if
t_{1}\overset{E}{=}t_{2}
and
s_{1}\overset{E}{=}s_{2}
, then
t_{1};s_{1}\overset{E}{=}t_{2};s_{2}

and
t_{1}\otimes s_{1}\overset{E}{=}t_{2}\otimes s_{2}
, whenever the composition is defined.

Note that the structural equations justify dropping all the dashed boxes when drawing the terms up to a term congruence.

Examples
2.40
-def:thy-indexed-monoids will play an important role when developing layered monoidal theories.

(Symmetric monoidal theory)
.

A
symmetric monoidal theory
is a monoidal theory
(C,\Sigma,\mathcal{S})
such that for all
a,b\in C
, the set
\Sigma(ab,ba)
contains the special generator, denoted by

, called the
symmetry
, and the set
\mathcal{S}
contains the following equations, where
s
ranges over all terms of the appropriate type, and the symmetry on the non-generator wires is defined recursively:

We remark that most of the concrete examples of monoidal theories we will see in this article will be symmetric.

(Theory of monoids)
.

The
theory of monoids
is the monoidal theory
(\{\bullet\},\Sigma,\mathcal{M})
with generators

and equations

=

.

Example 2.42

.

theory of comonoids

and equations

=
=
=

.

Example 2.43

(Theory with uniform comonoids)
.

We say that a symmetric monoidal theory
(C,\Sigma,\mathcal{U})
has
uniform comonoids
if every
a\in C
has a comonoid structure (i.e. the sets
\Sigma(a,aa)
and
\Sigma(a,\varepsilon)
contain the comonoid generators and
\mathcal{U}
contains the comonoid equations from Definition
2.42
), and upon extending the comonoid structure to all
w\in C^{*}
by the following recursion:

Example 2.44

(Theory with
1\mathchar 45\relax 1
-natural monoids)
.

We say that a symmetric monoidal theory
(C,\Sigma,\mathcal{N})
has
1\mathchar 45\relax 1
-natural monoids
if every
a\in C
has a monoid structure (i.e. the sets
\Sigma(aa,a)
and
\Sigma(\varepsilon,a)
contain the monoid generators and
\mathcal{N}
contains the monoid equations from Definition
2.41
), and for every
\sigma\in\Sigma(a,b)
with
a,b\in C
, we have the following equations:

Example 2.45

(Theory with indexed monoids)
.

We say that a symmetric monoidal theory has
indexed monoids
if it has both
1\mathchar 45\relax 1
-natural monoids (Definition
2.44
) and uniform comonoids (Definition
2.43
).

A model interprets a monoidal signature (or theory) in a strict monoidal category.

Definition 2.46
.

A
model
of a monoidal signature
(C,\Sigma)
is a strict monoidal category
(\mathcal{C},\otimes,I)
together with a function
i:C\rightarrow\mathcal{O}b(\mathcal{C})
, and for each
a,b\in C^{*}
, a function
i_{a,b}:\Sigma(a,b)\rightarrow\mathcal{C}(i^{*}a,i^{*}b)
.

We often denote a model of a monoidal signature
(C,\Sigma)
simply by
(\mathcal{C},i)
, where
\mathcal{C}
is a strict monoidal category, and
i
a family of functions as in the definition – referred to as the
interpretation functions
.

Definition 2.47
.

The category of
monoidal models

\mathbf{MMod}
has as objects quadruples
(C,\Sigma,\mathcal{C},i)
, where
(C,\Sigma)
is a monoidal signature and
(\mathcal{C},i)
its model. A morphism

(f,F):(C,\Sigma,\mathcal{C},i)\rightarrow(D,\Gamma,\mathcal{D},j)

is given by a morphism of monoidal signatures
f:(C,\Sigma)\rightarrow(D,\Gamma)
and a strict monoidal functor
F:\mathcal{C}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
such that the diagram on the left commutes (where
F_{0}
is the action of
F
on objects), and the diagram on the right commutes for all
a,b\in C^{*}
,

\mathcal{O}b(\mathcal{C})
C
i
\mathcal{O}b(\mathcal{D})
D
j
F_{0}
f
\mathcal{C}(i^{*}a,i^{*}b)
\Sigma(a,b)
i_{a,b}
\mathcal{D}(j^{*}f^{*}a,j^{*}f^{*}b)
\Gamma(f^{*}a,f^{*}b)
j_{f^{*}a,f^{*}b}
F
f_{a,b}

where we denote by
F
the appropriate restriction of the functor to the hom-set. Note that the restriction is indeed well-defined, as commutativity of the left diagram together with the fact that
F
is strict monoidal imply that
i^{*};F_{0}=f^{*};j^{*}
.

Given a model
(\mathcal{C},i)
of a monoidal signature
(C,\Sigma)
, it extends to a function from terms to the morphisms of
\mathcal{C}
, also denoted by
i:\texttt{Term}_{C,\Sigma}\rightarrow\mathcal{M}or(\mathcal{C})
, as follows:

\sigma:(a,b)\mapsto i_{a,b}(\sigma):(i^{*}a,i^{*}b)
,

\mathsf{id}_{a}:(a,a)\mapsto\mathsf{id}_{ia}:(ia,ia)
,

\mathsf{id}_{\varepsilon}:(\varepsilon,\varepsilon)\mapsto\mathsf{id}_{I}:(I,I)
,

(t;s):(a,c)\mapsto i(t);i(s):(i^{*}a,i^{*}c)
,

(t\otimes s):(ac,bd)\mapsto i(t)\otimes i(s):(i^{*}(ac),i^{*}(bd))
,

where
I
is the unit of
\mathcal{C}
, while
;
and
\otimes
on the right-hand side are the composition and the monoidal product of
\mathcal{C}
.

Definition 2.48
.

A
model
of a monoidal theory
(C,\Sigma,E)
is a model
(\mathcal{C},i)
of the monoidal signature
(C,\Sigma)
such that for all
(s,t)\in E
, we have
i(s)=i(t)
.

We denote by
\mathbf{MThMod}
the category of
models of monoidal theories
, whose objects are pairs of a monoidal theory and its model, and whose morphisms are pairs
(f,F)
such that
f
is a morphism of monoidal theories (hence, in particular, a morphism of monoidal signatures) and
(f,F)
is a morphism in
\mathbf{MMod}
.

We note that every model of a monoidal signature
(C,\Sigma)
can be viewed as a model of the monoidal theory
(C,\Sigma,\varnothing)
, so that
\mathbf{MMod}
can be identified with the full subcategory of
\mathbf{MThMod}
of theories with no equations.

We summarise the relationship between monoidal signatures, theories and their models in the following proposition.

.

Moreover, the objects in the fibre
\mathbf{MMod}(C,\Sigma)
are precisely the models of the signature
(C,\Sigma)
, and the objects in the fibre
\mathbf{MThMod}(\mathcal{T})
are precisely the models of the theory
\mathcal{T}
.

Proof.

The cartesian maps are those pairs whose monoidal functor part is (naturally isomorphic to) the identity functor.

Given an object
(C,\Sigma,E,\mathcal{C},i)\in\mathbf{MThMod}_{0}
and a morphism of monoidal theories
f:(D,\Gamma,F)\rightarrow(C,\Sigma,E)
, the cartesian lifting is given by
(f,\mathsf{id}_{\mathcal{C}}):(D,\Gamma,F,\mathcal{C},f;i)\rightarrow(C,\Sigma,E,\mathcal{C},i)
, where the interpretation functions of the domain model are given by
f;i:D\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
and

f_{a,b};i_{f^{*}a,f^{*}b}:\Gamma(a,b)\rightarrow\mathcal{C}(i^{*}f^{*}a,i^{*}f^{*}b).

For
\mathbf{MMod}\rightarrow\mathbf{MSgn}
, the situation is the same, except that all the theories are empty. It is then clear that the horizontal forgetful functors make the diagram commute, and that the top functor preserves cartesian liftings.
∎

Note that, while
\mathbf{MTh}\rightarrow\mathbf{MSgn}
is also a fibration, the functor
\mathbf{MThMod}\rightarrow\mathbf{MMod}
is
not
itself a fibration.

The usefulness of string diagrams lies in the fact that they are the
free models
of monoidal theories: an equation is derivable in the string diagrams of a monoidal theory if and only if it holds in all models of that theory.

Definition 2.50

(Term model)
.

Given a monoidal theory
\mathcal{T}=(C,\Sigma,E)
, the
term model
(or the
free model
)
F(\mathcal{T})
is the strict monoidal category defined by the following:

•

the objects are
C^{*}
,

•

the morphisms
a\rightarrow b
are the equivalence classes of terms with sort
(a,b)
under the term congruence
\overset{E}{=}
,

•

the composition of
[s]
and
[t]
is given by
[s;t]
,

•

the monoidal unit is the empty word
\varepsilon\in C^{*}
,

•

the monoidal product is given by concatenation on objects and by
\otimes
on morphisms.

We note that the operations
;
and
\otimes
above are well-defined since
\overset{E}{=}
is a congruence. The interpretation function
i:C\rightarrow C^{*}
sends the colour
a
to the one-element word
a
, and
i_{a,b}:\Sigma(a,b)\rightarrow F(\mathcal{T})(a,b)
sends each generator to its equivalence class.

For a monoidal signature
(C,\Sigma)
, we denote by
F(C,\Sigma)
the free model on the theory
(C,\Sigma,\varnothing)
.

Proposition 2.51
.

The term model construction extends to functors
F:\mathbf{MTh}\rightarrow\mathbf{MThMod}
and
F:\mathbf{MSgn}\rightarrow\mathbf{MMod}
, which are moreover the left adjoints to the respective forgetful functors.

Proof.

The action of the functor on morphisms is given by the recursive extension of the morphism of monoidal signatures to terms defined on page
2.7
.

The unit
\eta_{\mathcal{T}}:\mathcal{T}\rightarrow UF(\mathcal{T})=\mathcal{T}
is given by the identity
\mathsf{id}_{\mathcal{T}}
. The counit
\varepsilon_{\mathcal{T},\mathcal{M}}:(\mathcal{T},F(\mathcal{T}))=FU(\mathcal{T},\mathcal{M})\rightarrow(\mathcal{T},\mathcal{M})
, where we denote
\mathcal{M}\coloneq(\mathcal{C},i)
, is given by
(\mathsf{id}_{\mathcal{T}},i)
, where
i:F(\mathcal{T})\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
is given by
i^{*}
on objects, and on morphisms by the recursive extension of
i
to terms defined on page
2.7
.
∎

Corollary 2.52
.

For every monoidal theory
\mathcal{T}
and monoidal signature
(C,\Sigma)
, there are the following equivalences:

\displaystyle\mathbf{MThMod}(\mathcal{T})

\displaystyle\simeq\left.\raisebox{1.02228pt}{$F(\mathcal{T})$}\middle/\raisebox{-1.02228pt}{$\mathbf{MonCat}_{\mathsf{st}}$}\right.,

\displaystyle\mathbf{MMod}(C,\Sigma)

\displaystyle\simeq\left.\raisebox{1.02228pt}{$F(C,\Sigma)$}\middle/\raisebox{-1.02228pt}{$\mathbf{MonCat}_{\mathsf{st}}$}\right..

We conclude our discussion of models by pointing out that the notion of a model of a monoidal theory can be extended to non-strict monoidal categories upon interpreting the term congruence as isomorphism rather than equality. However, obtaining a free model via string diagrams is more involved in this case, as one needs to keep track of the isomorphisms capturing non-strict associativity and unitality. We refer the reader to Wilson, Ghica and Zanasi
29
;
30
for the details.

3
Layered theories

Here we define the syntax of layered monoidal theories, including the classes of
opfibrational
,
fibrational
and
deflational
theories in Subsection
3.1
. While the technical details here are sufficient to follow the theoretical developments, we refer the reader to Part I
19
for a more detailed discussion and examples. We remark that the terms
layered theory
and
layered monoidal theory
are used interchangeably; ditto the terms
layered signature
and
layered monoidal signature
.

Definition 3.1

(Layered signature)
.

A
layered signature
is a tuple
\left(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\left\{\mathcal{M}_{\omega}\right\}_{\omega\in\Omega}\right)
,
where
\Omega
is a set,
\mathcal{F}:\Omega\times\Omega\rightarrow\mathbf{Set}
is a function, and
\mathcal{M}_{\omega}
is a monoidal signature for each
\omega\in\Omega
.

Given a layered signature with monoidal signatures
\mathcal{M}_{\omega}
, we write
\mathcal{M}_{\omega}=(C_{\omega},\Sigma_{\omega})
. We often abbreviate a layered signature to
(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathcal{M}_{\omega})
, where the index
\omega
is implicitly assumed to range over
\Omega
. We refer to the elements of
\Omega
as
layers
and to the elements of
\mathcal{F}(\omega,\tau)
as
generators
with domain layer
\omega
and codomain layer
\tau
.

A
morphism of layered signatures

\left(F,F_{\tau,\omega},F^{\omega}\right):\left(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathcal{M}_{\omega}\right)\rightarrow\left(\Psi,\mathcal{G},\mathcal{M}_{\psi}\right)
is given by: (1) a function
F:\Omega\rightarrow\Psi
, (2) for every pair
(\omega,\tau)\in\Omega\times\Omega
, a function
F_{\omega,\tau}:\mathcal{F}(\omega,\tau)\rightarrow\mathcal{G}(F(\omega),F(\tau))
, and (3) for every
\omega\in\Omega
, a morphism of monoidal signatures
F^{\omega}:\mathcal{M}_{\omega}\rightarrow\mathcal{M}_{F(\omega)}
.

We denote the resulting category of layered signatures by
\mathbf{LSgn}
. As for the category of monoidal signatures
\mathbf{MSgn}
, we denote a morphism in
\mathbf{LSgn}
simply by
F:(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathcal{M}_{\omega})\rightarrow(\Psi,\mathcal{G},\mathcal{M}_{\psi})
as follows:
F:\Omega\rightarrow\Psi
(without subscripts or superscripts) denotes the function on layers,
F_{\omega,\tau}:\mathcal{F}(\omega,\tau)\rightarrow\mathcal{G}(F(\omega),F(\tau))
the functions on the generators, and
F^{\omega}:\mathcal{M}_{\omega}\rightarrow\mathcal{M}_{F(\omega)}
the morphisms of monoidal signatures.

Next, we define types, terms and 2-terms generated by a layered signature, summarised in the following table:

name

)

P^{0}_{\mathcal{L}}\subseteq\texttt{IntType}_{\mathcal{L}}\times\texttt{IntType}_{\mathcal{L}}
on the internal types as containing those terms which are in the same layer:
(A:\omega,B:\tau)\in P^{0}_{\mathcal{L}}

(T,S)\in P^{0}_{\mathcal{L}}

(F(T),F(S))\in P^{0}_{\mathcal{K}}
.

Definition 3.3

(0-equations)
.

Given a layered signature
\mathcal{L}

0-equations

We call the pairs of types
\texttt{Type}_{\mathcal{L}}\times\texttt{Type}_{\mathcal{L}}

.

Figure 2:
Rules for generating the basic terms of a layered signature

In the definition of a layered signature (Definition
3.1
), the generators between the layers are all of the type 1-1, i.e. the arity and coarity both consist of a single layer (this is in contrast to the generators within the layers, whose arity and coarity are lists of colours). This restriction is imposed as there is no uniform way to draw an arbitrary generator between a list (product) of layers. Since we do want the layers to interact, we introduce the mixed (co)arities at the level of terms. To this end, we need the notion of a
recursive sorting procedure
, which imposes some restrictions on what kinds of terms can be introduced. Each layered theory comes with a fixed recursive sorting procedure, within which the terms of the theory are generated.

Definition 3.5

(Recursive sorting procedure)
.

A
recursive sorting procedure
is a set of recursive rules such that

•

given a layered signature
\mathcal{L}
, the rules generate the set of expressions
\texttt{Term}^{1}_{\mathcal{L}}
called
terms
,

•

each term has a unique sort: we denote a term with its sort by
t:(T\mid S)
,

•

the set contains the rules for the
basic terms
of Figure
2
,

•

any additional rules do not change the set of internal terms, as defined in Definition
3.4
,

•

any morphism of layered signatures
F:\mathcal{L}\rightarrow\mathcal{K}
uniquely extends to a function
F:\texttt{Term}^{1}_{\mathcal{L}}\rightarrow\texttt{Term}^{1}_{\mathcal{K}}
by translating the types and terms in the assumption of each recursive rule, and then applying the corresponding rule in
\texttt{Term}^{1}_{\mathcal{K}}
, which is moreover consistent with the induced function on types:
t:(T\mid S)\mapsto F(t):(F(T)\mid F(S))
.

The additional rules we shall consider are given in Definition
3.18
as well as Figures
5
and
8
.

We say that two terms are
parallel
when they have the same sort, up to 0-equations, if there are any. Formally, given a set of 0-equations
E^{0}
, we define the binary relation
P^{1}_{\mathcal{L}}\subseteq\texttt{Term}^{1}_{\mathcal{L}}\times\texttt{Term}^{1}_{\mathcal{L}}
by
\left(t:(T_{t}\mid S_{t}),s:(T_{s}\mid S_{s})\right)\in P^{1}_{\mathcal{L}}
if and only if both
T_{t}\overset{0}{=}T_{s}
and
S_{t}\overset{0}{=}S_{s}
, and call the pairs of terms in
P^{1}_{\mathcal{L}}

parallel
with respect to
E^{0}
. Note that if
E^{0}
is empty (i.e. there are no equations), then terms are parallel if and only if they have the same sort.

Proposition 3.6
.

Let
F:(\mathcal{L},E^{0}_{\mathcal{L}})\rightarrow(\mathcal{K},E^{0}_{\mathcal{K}})
be a morphism of layered signatures such that the induced function on types
F:\texttt{Type}_{\mathcal{L}}\rightarrow\texttt{Type}_{\mathcal{K}}
preserves the chosen 0-equations. Then the induced function on terms
F:\texttt{Term}^{1}_{\mathcal{L}}\rightarrow\texttt{Term}^{1}_{\mathcal{K}}
preserves parallel terms: if
(s,t)\in P^{1}_{\mathcal{L}}
, then
(F(s),F(t))\in P^{1}_{\mathcal{K}}
.

Proof.

By the fact that terms with the same sort are mapped to the terms with the same sort, and by induction on the construction of the type congruence.
∎

Definition 3.7

(1-equations)
.

Given a layered signature
\mathcal{L}
together with a recursive sorting procedure and a set of 0-equations
E^{0}
, a set of
1-equations
with respect to
E^{0}
is a subset
E^{1}\subseteq P^{1}_{\mathcal{L}}
.

Given a set of 1-equations
E^{1}
, we extend it to the
term congruence

\overset{1}{=}
, i.e. the smallest equivalence relation on
P^{1}_{\mathcal{L}}
containing
E^{1}
that is preserved by the recursive rules in Figure
2
.

Definition 3.8

(Choice of 2-cells)
.

Given a layered signature
\mathcal{L}
together with a recursive sorting procedure and a set of 0-equations
E^{0}
, a
choice of 2-cells
with respect to
E^{0}
is a function
\eta:P^{1}_{\mathcal{L}}\rightarrow\mathbf{Set}
, assigning to each parallel pair of terms a set of
generating 2-cells
.

Note that any layered signature in the sense of Definition
3.1
can be seen as having a choice of 2-cells by setting
\eta
to be the constant function returning the empty set. A morphism between layered signatures with a choice of 2-cells
(F,F^{2}):(\mathcal{L},E^{0}_{\mathcal{L}},\eta_{\mathcal{L}})\rightarrow(\mathcal{K},E^{0}_{\mathcal{K}},\eta_{\mathcal{K}})
is given by a morphism of layered signatures
F:\mathcal{L}\rightarrow\mathcal{K}
such that the induced function
F:\texttt{Type}_{\mathcal{L}}\rightarrow\texttt{Type}_{\mathcal{K}}
preserves the 0-equations, and for each pair
(t,s)\in P^{1}_{\mathcal{L}}
, a function
F^{2}_{t,s}:\eta_{\mathcal{L}}(t,s)\rightarrow\eta_{\mathcal{K}}(F(t),F(s))
.

Definition 3.9

(2-terms)
.

Given a layered signature
\mathcal{L}
with a choice of 2-cells
\eta
, a
2-term
is an expression of the form
\alpha:(s,t)
, where
(s,t)\in P^{1}_{\mathcal{L}}
is its
sort
, generated by the following recursive procedure:

a\in\eta(t,s)

a:(t,s)

t\in\texttt{Term}^{1}_{\mathcal{L}}

\mathsf{id}_{t}:(t,t)

\alpha:(t,s)

\beta:(s,k)

\alpha;\beta:(t,k)

\alpha:(t_{1},s_{1})

\beta:(t_{2},s_{2})

\alpha\otimes\beta:(t_{1}\otimes t_{2},s_{1}\otimes s_{2})

\alpha:(t_{1},s_{1})

\beta:(t_{2},s_{2})

t_{1}:(T\mid S)

t_{2}:(S\mid K)

.

\alpha*\beta:(t_{1};t_{2},s_{1};s_{2})

Akin to terms, we denote the set of 2-terms by
\texttt{Term}^{2}_{\mathcal{L}}
.

Remark 3.10
.

We have chosen not to extend the 2-terms to the recursively defined internal terms (i.e. the ones generated by the rules
and
). There is no inherent reason for omitting these terms: upon adding them, one would just need to add the corresponding structural 2-equations (see Definition
3.17
). However, in the models we will consider the 2-categorical structure only arises at the level of external terms, or does not need to be propagated between layers. Thus, for the sake of slightly reducing the complexity of the current presentation, we omit these terms. Moreover, in deflational theories, such terms are automatically induced by the external ones: see Corollary
(
19
, Corollary 4.4)
.

Let
(F,F^{2}):(\mathcal{L},E^{0}_{\mathcal{L}},\eta_{\mathcal{L}})\rightarrow(\mathcal{K},E^{0}_{\mathcal{K}},\eta_{\mathcal{K}})
be a morphism between layered signatures with a choice of 2-cells. The functions between the generating 2-cells
F^{2}_{t,s}
then yield a function
F^{2}:\texttt{Term}^{2}_{\mathcal{L}}\rightarrow\texttt{Term}^{2}_{\mathcal{K}}
recursively defined as follows:

\displaystyle a:(t,s)

\displaystyle\mapsto F^{2}_{t,s}(a):(F(t),F(s))

\displaystyle\mathsf{id}_{t}:(t,t)

\displaystyle\mapsto\mathsf{id}_{F(t)}:(F(t),F(t))

\displaystyle\alpha\otimes\beta:(t_{1}\otimes t_{2},s_{1}\otimes s_{2})

\displaystyle\mapsto F^{2}(\alpha)\otimes F^{2}(\beta):(F(t_{1})\otimes F(t_{2}),F(s_{1})\otimes F(s_{2}))

\displaystyle\alpha;\beta:(t,k)

\displaystyle\mapsto F^{2}(\alpha);F^{2}(\beta):(F(t),F(k))

\displaystyle\alpha*\beta:(t_{1};t_{2},s_{1};s_{2})

\displaystyle\mapsto F^{2}(\alpha)*F^{2}(\beta):(F(t_{1});F(t_{2}),F(s_{1});F(s_{2})).

As for the terms, given a set of 1-equations
E^{1}
, a pair of 2-terms is in the
parallel 2-term relation

P^{2}_{\mathcal{L}}
with respect to
E^{1}
if and only if both 2-terms have the same sort up to the 1-equations:
\left(\alpha:(t_{\alpha},s_{\alpha}),\beta:(t_{\beta},s_{\beta})\right)\in P^{2}_{\mathcal{L}}
if and only if both
t_{\alpha}\overset{1}{=}t_{\beta}
and
s_{\alpha}\overset{1}{=}s_{\beta}
. We draw a 2-term
\alpha:(t,s)
either as

T
S
t
s
\alpha

, or simply as an arrow
t\xrightarrow{\alpha}s
(see e.g. Figure
9
on page
9
).

Proposition 3.11
.

Let
(F,F^{2}):(\mathcal{L},E^{0}_{\mathcal{L}},\eta_{\mathcal{L}},E^{1}_{\mathcal{L}})\rightarrow(\mathcal{K},E^{0}_{\mathcal{K}},\eta_{\mathcal{K}},E^{1}_{\mathcal{K}})

be a morphism between layered signatures with a choice of 2-cells such that the induced function on terms
F:\texttt{Term}^{1}_{\mathcal{L}}\rightarrow\texttt{Term}^{1}_{\mathcal{K}}
preserves the specified 1-equations. Then the induced function on 2-terms
F^{2}:\texttt{Term}^{2}_{\mathcal{L}}\rightarrow\texttt{Term}^{2}_{\mathcal{K}}
preserves parallel terms: if
(\alpha,\beta)\in P^{2}_{\mathcal{L}}
, then
(F^{2}(\alpha),F^{2}(\beta))\in P^{2}_{\mathcal{K}}
.

Proof.

By the fact that 2-terms with the same sort are mapped to 2-terms with the same sort, and by induction on the construction of the term congruence.
∎

Definition 3.12

(2-equations)
.

Let
\mathcal{L}
be layered signature with a set of 0-equations
E^{0}
. Given a set of 1-equations
E^{1}
and a choice of 2-cells
\eta
with respect to
E^{0}
, a set of
2-equations
with respect to
E^{1}
and
\eta
is a subset
E^{2}\subseteq P^{2}_{\mathcal{L}}
.

Given a set of 2-equations
E^{2}
, we extend it to the
2-term congruence

\overset{2}{=}
, i.e. the smallest equivalence relation on
P^{2}_{\mathcal{L}}
containing
E^{2}
that is preserved by the recursive rules in Definition
3.9
.

We now have all the ingredients to define a layered theory.

Definition 3.13

(Layered theory)
.

Let us fix a recursive sorting procedure (Definition
3.5
). A
layered theory

(\mathcal{L},E^{0},E^{1},\eta,E^{2})
consists of the following: a layered signature
\mathcal{L}
(Definition
3.1
), a set of 0-equations
E^{0}
(Definition
3.3
), a set of 1-equations
E^{1}
with respect to
E^{0}
(Definition
3.7
), a choice of 2-cells
\eta
with respect to
E^{0}
(Definition
3.8
), a set of 2-equations
E^{2}
with respect to
E^{1}
and
\eta
(Definition
3.12
).

For a fixed recursive sorting procedure, a
morphism of layered theories

(F,F^{2}):(\mathcal{L},E^{0}_{\mathcal{L}},E^{1}_{\mathcal{L}},\eta_{\mathcal{L}},E^{2}_{\mathcal{L}})\rightarrow(\mathcal{K},E^{0}_{\mathcal{K}},E^{1}_{\mathcal{K}},\eta_{\mathcal{K}},E^{2}_{\mathcal{K}})

is given by a morphism of layered signatures with a choice of 2-cells
(F,F^{2})
(thus, in particular, the induced function
F:\texttt{Type}_{\mathcal{L}}\rightarrow\texttt{Type}_{\mathcal{K}}
preserves the 0-equations), such that the induced functions
F:\texttt{Term}^{1}_{\mathcal{L}}\rightarrow\texttt{Term}^{1}_{\mathcal{K}}
and
F^{2}:\texttt{Term}^{2}_{\mathcal{L}}\rightarrow\texttt{Term}^{2}_{\mathcal{K}}
preserve the 1-equations and the 2-equations, respectively. We denote any category of layered theories by
\mathbf{LTh}
: note that each recursive sorting procedure results in a different category.

Proposition 3.14
.

Let us fix a recursive sorting procedure. The forgetful functor
\mathbf{LTh}\rightarrow\mathbf{LSgn}
is a fibration. Moreover, the objects in the fibre
\mathbf{LTh}(\mathcal{L})
are precisely the layered theories with the signature
\mathcal{L}
.

Next, we define the structural equations that will be used to define the free models.

Definition 3.15

(Structural 0-equations)
.

Given a layered signature, the
structural 0-equations

S^{0}
are given by:

\displaystyle(AB)C:\omega

\displaystyle=A(BC):\omega,

\displaystyle\varepsilon A:\omega

\displaystyle=A:\omega=A\varepsilon:\omega,

\displaystyle f(AB):\tau

\displaystyle=f(A)f(B):\tau,

\displaystyle f(\varepsilon):\tau

\displaystyle=\varepsilon:\tau.

Definition 3.19

(Externally symmetric layered theory)
.

A layered theory is
externally symmetric
if it has the symmetry terms, and the structural 0-equations (Definition
3.15
) and 1-equations (Definition
3.16
) hold, and the 1-equations contain the equations for symmetric monoidal theories in Definition
2.40
for the symmetry terms.

3.1
Opfibrational, fibrational and deflational theories

Opfibrational theories are defined for the recursive procedure specified in Definition
3.20
and have no generating 2-cells.

Figure 5:
Rules for generating the opfibrational terms

Definition 3.20

(Opfibrational layered theory)
.

We say that a layered theory is
opfibrational
if it has no generating 2-cells, and its recursive sorting procedure consists of the rules in Figure
5
and the symmetry terms of Definition
3.18
(in addition to the basic terms in Figure
2
).

The intuition behind the opfibrational terms is that we take an “external” view of the monoidal categories and monoidal functors between them. In more detail:

•

the terms
and
capture the monoidal product and unit in the layer
\omega
: e.g. sliding the internal terms through the term
defines the monoidal product on morphisms (see Figure
6
),

•

the terms

Remark 3.21
.

A more accurate name for the theories of Definition
3.20
would be a
strict layered theory for opfibrations with indexed monoids
. Since this is somewhat cumbersome, and we shall not consider any other layered theories featuring an opfibration, we stick to the term
opfibrational
.

We denote the resulting category of opfibrational layered theories by
\mathbf{OpFTh}
. In this case the morphisms are simply equation preserving morphisms of signatures rather than pairs of morphisms, as there are no generating 2-cells.
