Figure 8:
Rules for generating the fibrational terms

The structural fibrational equations are likewise obtained by dualising the structural opfibrational equations (Definition
3.22
). For the sake of completeness, and since they will be used for defining the structural deflational equations, we state the definition explicitly.

Definition 3.23

(Structural fibrational equations)
.

By the
structural fibrational equations
we mean the structural equations, the external symmetry equations, as well as the following sets of 1-equations, where “dual” and “dualising” means reflecting the terms horizontally: (1) the equations of uniform monoids (the dual of Definition
2.43
) for the terms
and
, (2) the defining identities of monoidal categories obtained by dualising Figure
6
, and (3) the defining identities of monoidal functors obtained by dualising Figure
7
.

With these modifications, any properties of fibrational theories can be obtained by dualising the corresponding properties of opfibrational theories: all the diagrams are simply reversed.

We now arrive to our last – and most important – class of theories. Deflational theories can be thought of as glueing an opfibrational and a fibrational theory together along the internal terms.

Definition 3.24

(Deflational layered theory)
.

A layered theory is
deflational
if its recursive sorting procedure consists of the rules for the symmetry terms of Definition
3.18
, as well as of the rules for opfibrational and fibrational terms in Figures
5
and
8
(in addition to the basic terms in Figure
2
).

We denote the category of deflational layered theories by
\mathbf{DeflTh}
. In a deflational theory, every opfibrational term
x:(T\mid S)
generated by a rule in Figure
5
has a corresponding fibrational term
\bar{x}:(S\mid T)
generated by the corresponding rule in Figure
8
. We use this to define the
structural 2-cells
, expressing
\bar{x}
as the right adjoint to
x
.

Definition 3.25

(Structural 2-cells)
.

Given a deflational layered theory with layered signature
\mathcal{L}
, the
structural 2-cells
are given by the choice of 2-cells
\eta_{\mathsf{str}}
defined as follows: for every opfibrational term
x:(T\mid S)
generated by a rule in Figure
5
one has
\eta_{\mathsf{str}}\left(\mathsf{id}_{T},x;\bar{x}\right)\coloneq\{\eta_{x}\}
,
\eta_{\mathsf{str}}\left(\bar{x};x,\mathsf{id}_{S}\right)\coloneq\{\varepsilon_{x}\}
, and
\eta_{\mathsf{str}}
returns the empty set otherwise.

We display the 10 structural 2-cells explicitly in Figure
9
: the left-hand side contains the unit 2-cells (
\eta_{x}
), while the right-hand side contains the counit 2-cells (
\varepsilon_{x}
). We consistently omit the labels of the structural 2-cells, as the domain and the codomain determine them uniquely.

\blacktriangleleft_{f}
\vartriangleright_{f}
\blacktriangleleft_{f}
\vartriangleright_{f}

Figure 9:
Structural 2-cells for deflational theories

Definition 3.26

(Structural deflational equations)
.

By the
structural deflational equations
we mean: the structural opfibrational equations (Definition
3.22
), the structural fibrational equations (Definition
3.23
) and the following 2-equations for each opfibrational term
x:(T\mid S)
and all terms
y:(T\mid T)
and
z:(S\mid S)
that are either internal or a product (obtained by the
) of internal terms:

\displaystyle\left(\eta_{x}*\mathsf{id}_{x}\right);\left(\mathsf{id}_{x}*\varepsilon_{x}\right)

\displaystyle=\mathsf{id}_{x}

\displaystyle\left(\mathsf{id}_{\bar{x}}*\eta_{x}\right);\left(\varepsilon_{x}*\mathsf{id}_{\bar{x}}\right)

\displaystyle=\mathsf{id}_{\bar{x}}

\displaystyle\mathsf{id}_{y}*\eta_{x}

\displaystyle=\eta_{x}*\mathsf{id}_{y}

\displaystyle\mathsf{id}_{z}*\varepsilon_{x}

\displaystyle=\varepsilon_{x}*\mathsf{id}_{z}.

We denote the structural deflational 1- and 2-equations by
S_{\mathsf{defl}}^{1}
and
S_{\mathsf{defl}}^{2}
.

Note that the structural deflational equations contain, in particular, the structural 0-, 1- and 2-equations of Definitions
3.15
,
3.16
and
3.17
. The additional 2-equations that are required to hold are the usual zigzag equations defining an adjunction (see Definition
5.1
for their graphical depiction), as well as the equations stating the compatibility of the structural 2-cells with the “sliding through” 1-equations for internal terms in Figures
6
and
7
.

4
Indexed monoids

In this section, we study categories with indexed monoids (Definition
4.4
). We ultimately extend this notion to opfibrations with indexed monoids (Definition
4.13
), a special case of which will be used as a semantics for opfibrational theories in Section
6.1
.

A symmetric monoidal category is denoted by
(\mathcal{C},\otimes,I,\alpha,\lambda,\rho,\sigma)
, where
I
is the monoidal unit, while the Greek letters denote the natural isomorphisms:
\alpha
is the associator,
\lambda
and
\rho
are, respectively, the left and right unitors, while
\sigma
is the symmetry. For brevity, we shall leave the natural isomorphisms implicit, and simply write
(\mathcal{C},\otimes,I)
for a monoidal category. We take the liberty to use string diagrams even when reasoning about non-strict monoidal categories: we trust that the reader will be able to infer the missing natural isomorphisms where necessary.

4.1
Categories with indexed monoids

Here we define categories with indexed monoids, and show that free models of monoidal theories with indexed monoids give the left adjoint to the forgetful functor from the categories with indexed monoids to categories.

The following definition should be compared to Definition
2.43
, where we defined the monoidal theory with uniform comonoids.

Definition 4.1

(Uniform comonoids)
.

A symmetric monoidal category
(\mathcal{C},\otimes,I)
has
uniform comonoids
if the following obtain:

•

for every object
x\in\mathcal{O}b(\mathcal{C})
, there are morphisms
d_{x}:x\rightarrow x\otimes x
and
e_{x}:x\rightarrow I
,

•

for every object
x
, the morphism
d_{x}
is a comonoid with the counit
e_{x}
(up to the natural isomorphisms),

•

d_{I}=\rho_{I}^{-1}
and
e_{I}=\mathsf{id}_{1}
,

•

d
and
e
are natural, i.e. for every morphism
f:x\rightarrow y
, we have
d_{x};(f\otimes f)=f;d_{y}
and
f;e_{y}=e_{x}
,

•

for all objects
x,y\in\mathcal{O}b(\mathcal{C})
, we have (up to associators)
(d_{x}\otimes d_{y});(\mathsf{id}_{x}\otimes\sigma_{xy}\otimes\mathsf{id}_{y})=d_{x\otimes y}
.

Note that the naturality conditions imply that the uniform comonoids are unique, in the sense that if both
(d,e)
and
(d^{\prime},e^{\prime})
are uniform comonoids on the same symmetric monoidal category, then
(d,e)=(d^{\prime},e^{\prime})
. The following result is known as
Fox’s theorem
. We refer the reader to Melliès
(
22
, Section 6.4)
for a more detailed discussion, including more refined versions of the equivalence.

Proposition 4.2
.

A symmetric monoidal category
(\mathcal{C},\otimes,I)
is cartesian monoidal (i.e.
\otimes
is the cartesian product and
I
is the terminal object) if and only if it has uniform comonoids.

Proof.

Suppose
(\mathcal{C},\otimes,I)
has uniform comonoids
(d,e)

and
g
as below

}.

Finally, observe that
I
is the terminal object by naturality of
e
.

Conversely, if
(\mathcal{C},\otimes,I)
is cartesian monoidal, then
d_{x}
is the diagonal and
e_{x}
is the unique map into the terminal object.
∎

Definition 4.3

(Consistent monoids)
.

Consistent monoids
in a symmetric monoidal category
(\mathcal{C},\otimes,I)
consist of the following data:

•

for every object
x\in\mathcal{O}b(\mathcal{C})
, there are morphisms
m_{x}:x\otimes x\rightarrow x
and
u_{x}:I\rightarrow x
,

•

for every object
x
, the morphism
m_{x}
is a monoid with the unit
u_{x}
(up to the natural isomorphisms),

•

m_{I}=\rho_{I}
and
u_{I}=\mathsf{id}_{I}
,

•

u
is natural, i.e. for every morphism
f:x\rightarrow y
, we have
u_{x};f=u_{y}
,

•

for all objects
x,y\in\mathcal{O}b(\mathcal{C})
, we have (up to associators)
(\mathsf{id}_{x}\otimes\sigma_{yx}\otimes\mathsf{id}_{y});(m_{x}\otimes m_{y})=m_{x\otimes y}
.

Similarly to uniform comonoids, the units of consistent monoids are unique: in fact, naturality and
u_{I}=\mathsf{id}_{I}
imply that
I
is the initial object. Contrariwise, since naturality is not asked of monoid multiplication, they need not be unique, and therefore correspond to a choice of structure rather than being a property of a category. This motivates the following definition.

Definition 4.4

(Indexed monoids)
.

We call a choice of consistent monoids in a symmetric monoidal category with uniform comonoids
indexed monoids
. We denote a
category with indexed monoids
by
(\mathcal{C},\otimes,I,m)
.

Using Fox’s theorem (Proposition
4.2
), we restate the definition of a category with indexed monoids as follows.

Proposition 4.5
.

A symmetric monoidal category
(\mathcal{C},\otimes,I)
has indexed monoids if

•

it is cartesian monoidal,

•

I
is also an initial object (thus a zero object),

•

for every object
x\in\mathcal{O}b(\mathcal{C})
, there is a monoid
m_{x}:x\otimes x\rightarrow x
with unit
u_{x}:I\rightarrow x
,

•

m_{I}=\rho_{I}
,

•

for all objects
x,y\in\mathcal{O}b(\mathcal{C})
, we have (up to associators)
(\mathsf{id}_{x}\otimes\sigma_{yx}\otimes\mathsf{id}_{y});(m_{x}\otimes m_{y})=m_{x\otimes y}
.

Example 4.6
.

Let
(\mathbf{Vect}_{k},\oplus,\{0\})
be the category of vector spaces over a fixed field
k
, with the direct sum as the monoidal product. Then, for every vector space
V
, addition of vectors
+:V\oplus V\rightarrow V
gives an indexed monoid structure. This example generalises to any semiadditive category.

Example 4.7
.

Consider the forgetful functor
U:\mathbf{Mon}\rightarrow\mathbf{Set}_{*}
from the category of monoids to the category of pointed sets. Define the category
U\mathchar 45\relax\mathbf{Mon}
to have the same objects as
\mathbf{Mon}
, and the hom-sets as
U\mathchar 45\relax\mathbf{Mon}(M,N)\coloneqq\mathbf{Set}_{*}(UM,UN)
, i.e. the maps are required to preserve the monoidal unit, but not the binary operation. The category
U\mathchar 45\relax\mathbf{Mon}
has a cartesian monoidal structure given by the product of monoids, the zero object is the monoid with one element, and for every monoid
M=(X,\cdot,1)
, we define the morphism
m_{M}:M\times M\rightarrow M
by the multiplication of the monoid:
(x,y)\mapsto x\cdot y
. This gives
U\mathchar 45\relax\mathbf{Mon}
an indexed monoid structure.

Let us denote by
\mathbf{IMon}
the category whose objects are symmetric monoidal categories with indexed monoids, and whose morphisms are strong monoidal functors
(F,\mu):(\mathcal{C},\otimes,I,m)\rightarrow(\mathcal{D},\otimes,I,m)
such that for all
x\in\mathcal{O}b(\mathcal{C})
, we have
\mu_{xx};F(m_{x})=m_{Fx}
.

Definition 4.8
.

Let
\mathcal{I}=(\mathcal{C},\otimes,I,m)
be a category with indexed monoids. A morphism
f:x\rightarrow y
in
\mathcal{C}
is a
monoid homomorphism
if
m_{x};f=(f\otimes f);m_{y}
. We denote the set of monoid homomorphisms by
\hom(\mathcal{I})
.

Proposition 4.9
.

The monoid homomorphisms in a category with indexed monoids form a wide monoidal subcategory. Moreover, the monoid homomorphisms are preserved by the morphisms in
\mathbf{IMon}
.

Proof.

The identity morphisms are evidently monoid homomorphisms. Closure under composition and monoidal products follows from the defining equation of monoid homomorphisms and the consistency requirement. Preservation of a monoid homomorphism
f:x\rightarrow y
under a functor
(F,\mu)
in
\mathbf{IMon}
amounts to the equation
m_{Fx};Ff=(Ff\otimes Ff);m_{Fy}
, which we obtain as the commutativity of the following diagram:

We define the functor
\hom:\mathbf{IMon}\rightarrow\mathbf{Cat}
by mapping each
\mathcal{I}
to
\hom(\mathcal{I})
, and each functor to its restriction to monoid homomorphisms. We conclude this section by showing that the monoid homomorphism functor so defined has a left adjoint, obtained by freely adding indexed monoids.

(Theory with indexed monoids generated by a category)
.

and all

,

:

Definition 4.11

(Free category with indexed monoids)
.

Let
\mathcal{X}
be a small category. The
free category with indexed monoids generated by
\mathcal{X}
is the term model (Definition
2.50
)
F_{\mathsf{im}}(\mathcal{X})
of the theory with indexed monoids generated by
\mathcal{X}
(Definition
4.10
).

Proposition 4.12
.

In the situation of Definition
4.11
, the interpretation functions
i:\mathcal{O}b(\mathcal{X})\rightarrow\mathcal{O}b(\mathcal{X})^{*}
and
i_{a,b}:\mathcal{X}(a,b)\rightarrow F_{\mathsf{im}}(\mathcal{X})(a,b)
define a functor
i:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\hom\left(F_{\mathsf{im}}(\mathcal{X})\right)
. Moreover, the functor
i
satisfies the following universal property: for every category with indexed monoids
\mathcal{I}
and a functor
G:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\hom\left(\mathcal{I}\right)
in
\mathbf{Cat}
, there is a unique (up to a monoidal natural isomorphism) morphism
\bar{G}:F_{\mathsf{im}}(\mathcal{X})\rightarrow\mathcal{I}
in
\mathbf{IMon}
such that the diagram

\mathcal{X}
\hom\left(F_{\mathsf{im}}(\mathcal{X})\right)
\hom\left(\mathcal{I}\right)
G
i
\hom\left(\bar{G}\right)

commutes; thus exhibiting
F_{\mathsf{im}}
as the left adjoint to
\hom:\mathbf{IMon}\rightarrow\mathbf{Cat}
.

Proof.

Functoriality of
i
follows from the equations in Definition
4.10
. The fact that
i_{a,b}(f)=f
is a monoid homomorphism is part of the definition of a theory with
1\mathchar 45\relax 1
-natural monoids (Definition
2.44
).

When defining a morphism
\bar{G}:F_{\mathsf{im}}(\mathcal{X})\rightarrow\mathcal{I}
in
\mathbf{IMon}
, the only freedoms we have is choosing where to map the colours (objects of
\mathcal{X}
) and the generators that are not part of the indexed monoid structure (the morphisms in
\hom\left(F_{\mathsf{im}}(\mathcal{X})\right)
), both of which are uniquely (up to the structural isomorphisms of
\mathcal{I}
) determined by commutativity of the diagram.
∎

4.2
Opfibrations with indexed monoids

Here we extend the notion of indexed monoids from categories to opfibrations. The central notion is that of an
opfibration with indexed monoids
, or
im-opfibration
, which is shown to be very closely related to monoids in the category of split opfibrations
\mathbf{MonOpFib}_{\mathsf{sp}}(\mathcal{X})
(Theorem
4.16
). We choose to work with opfibrations rather than fibrations, however, all the developments dualise to fibrations, in which the appropriate notion is
indexed comonoids
rather than indexed monoids.

Definition 4.13

(Im-opfibration)
.

We say that an opfibration
\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow\mathcal{X}

has indexed monoids
if the base category
\mathcal{X}
has indexed monoids,
\mathcal{Y}
is cartesian monoidal, the functor preserves and reflects the cartesian products, and the cartesian product of opcartesian maps in
\mathcal{Y}
is opcartesian. For the sake of brevity, we refer to an opfibration with indexed monoids as an
im-opfibration
.

Note that in the above definition,
\mathcal{X}
having indexed monoids implies that
\mathcal{X}
is cartesian, so that it makes sense to ask the functor to preserve and reflect the cartesian products.

An im-opfibration is
split
if it is a split opfibration and the chosen cartesian products are preserved and reflected strictly.

Definition 4.14

(Morphism of im-opfibrations)
.

A
morphism of im-opfibrations
is a morphism of opfibrations
(H,K)
such that the functor between the base categories
K
is a morphism in
\mathbf{IMon}
, and the functor between the total categories
H
preserves the cartesian monoidal structure.

A morphism of split im-opfibrations is a morphism of split opfibrations such that both functors are strict monoidal. Let us denote the category of im-opfibrations by
\mathbf{imOpFib}
, and the fixed base case by
\mathbf{imOpFib}(\mathcal{X})
. As for (op)fibrations, the subcategory of split im-opfibrations is denoted by adding the subscript
\mathsf{sp}
in each case.

Given an im-opfibration
\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow\mathcal{X}
, define its
restriction
as the functor
\mathcal{Y}^{*}\rightarrow\hom(\mathcal{X})
, where
\hom(\mathcal{X})
is the subcategory of monoid homomorphisms, and
\mathcal{Y}^{*}
is the wide subcategory of
\mathcal{Y}^{*}
defined by
F\in\mathcal{Y}^{*}
if and only if the image of
F
is in
\hom(\mathcal{X})
, while the action of the functor is given by that of the original functor.

Proposition 4.15
.

For any im-opfibration
\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow\mathcal{X}
, its restriction
\mathcal{Y}^{*}\rightarrow\hom(\mathcal{X})
is an opfibration. Moreover, the restriction extends to a functor
\hom:\mathbf{imOpFib}\rightarrow\mathbf{OpFib}
.

Proof.

The opcartesian maps are inherited by restriction:
F\in\mathcal{Y}^{*}
is opcartesian if and only if
F\in\mathcal{Y}
is opcartesian. The opcartesian liftings are likewise given by opcartesian liftings in
\mathcal{Y}
. The morphisms restrict to morphisms of opfibrations by Proposition
4.9
.
∎

Theorem 4.16
.

Let
\mathcal{X}
be a small category. The category of split opfibrations with monoids with base
\mathcal{X}
is equivalent to the category of split im-opfibrations with base
F_{\mathsf{im}}(\mathcal{X})
:

\mathbf{MonOpFib}_{\mathsf{sp}}(\mathcal{X})\simeq\mathbf{imOpFib}_{\mathsf{sp}}(F_{\mathsf{im}}(\mathcal{X})).

Proof.

Given a split opfibration
\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow\mathcal{X}
with a monoid

\lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}
}.

The action of the functor
\mathcal{Y}_{\otimes}\rightarrow F_{\mathsf{im}}(\mathcal{X})
is defined by extending
\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow\mathcal{X}
to cartesian products, and by mapping the newly added generators to the freely added monoid multiplication and unit in the base. The opcartesian morphisms in
\mathcal{Y}_{\otimes}
are generated as follows:

•

if
f\in\mathcal{Y}
is opcartesian, then so is
f\in\mathcal{Y}_{\otimes}
,

•

the newly added generators are opcartesian,

•

if
f
and
g
are opcartesian, then so are the composition
f;g
(whenever defined) and the cartesian product
f\times g
.

It is then straightforward to construct the opcartesian liftings. Since the cartesian structure is preserved and reflected by construction, we indeed obtain an im-opfibration.

Conversely, given a split im-opfibration
\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow F_{\mathsf{im}}(\mathcal{X})
, we proceed to define a monoid

\mathcal{Y}^{*}
\mathcal{Y}^{*}\boxtimes\mathcal{Y}^{*}
\otimes_{\mathcal{Y}}
\mathcal{X}
\mathcal{Y}^{*}
\mathcal{X}
\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{Y}}
\mathcal{X}
\mathsf{id}_{\mathcal{X}}

on the split opfibration
\mathcal{Y}^{*}\rightarrow\mathcal{X}
, where
\mathcal{Y}^{*}
is the wide subcategory of
\mathcal{Y}
obtained by restriction, i.e.
F\in\mathcal{Y}^{*}
if and only if the image of
F
is in
\mathcal{X}
. First, observe that, since the cartesian products are strictly preserved and reflected, for all morphisms
f,g\in\mathcal{X}
, we have
\mathcal{Y}_{f}\times\mathcal{Y}_{g}\simeq\mathcal{Y}_{f\times g}
, and the isomorphism is given (from left to right) by the action of the product functor on
\mathcal{Y}
. Further, each
f:x\rightarrow y
in
\mathcal{X}
is a monoid homomorphism by construction of
F_{\mathsf{im}}(\mathcal{X})
, which induces a function
\mathcal{Y}_{f\times f}\rightarrow\mathcal{Y}_{f}
by the universal property of the opcartesian liftings of the monoid multiplication on
x
. Hence, for every morphism
f\in\mathcal{X}
, we define the mapping
\otimes_{f}:\mathcal{Y}_{f}\times\mathcal{Y}_{f}\rightarrow\mathcal{Y}_{f}
by composing the isomorphism
\mathcal{Y}_{f}\times\mathcal{Y}_{f}\simeq\mathcal{Y}_{f\times f}
with the function
\mathcal{Y}_{f\times f}\rightarrow\mathcal{Y}_{f}
. We now define the functor
\otimes_{\mathcal{Y}}:\mathcal{Y}^{*}\boxtimes\mathcal{Y}^{*}\rightarrow\mathcal{Y}^{*}
as the disjoint union of these mappings:
\otimes_{\mathcal{Y}}\coloneq\coprod_{f\in\mathcal{X}}\otimes_{f}
. Next, once again by strict preservation and reflection of cartesian products, we have that
\mathcal{Y}_{I}=\{I\}
, so that the reindexing functor
\mathbf{1}_{x}:\mathcal{Y}_{I}\rightarrow\mathcal{Y}_{x}
induced by the monoidal unit on
x
constitutes a choice of an object in
\mathcal{Y}_{x}
, which we denote by
\mathbf{1}(x)
. Moreover, the reindexing functor
f^{*}:\mathcal{Y}_{x}\rightarrow\mathcal{Y}_{w}
induced by a morphism
f:x\rightarrow w
in
\mathcal{X}
preserves these chosen object in the sense that
f^{*}(\mathbf{1}(x))=\mathbf{1}(w)
. We thus define the unit functor
\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{Y}}:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{Y}^{*}
by
x\mapsto\mathbf{1}(x)
on objects and by the opcartesian liftings on morphisms. Associativity and unitality are now induced by associativity and unitality of the monoids in
F_{\mathsf{im}}(\mathcal{X})
, so that
(\mathcal{Y}^{*},\otimes_{\mathcal{Y}},\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{Y}})
indeed defines a monoid in
(\mathbf{OpFib}_{\mathsf{sp}}(\mathcal{X}),\boxtimes,\mathsf{id}_{\mathcal{X}})
.

Applying the monoid construction to the im-opfibration obtained from a monoid recovers the original monoid:
\otimes_{\mathcal{Y}_{\otimes}}=\otimes
and
\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{Y}_{\otimes}}=\mathbf{1}
, since the restriction of
\mathcal{Y}_{\otimes}
is
\mathcal{Y}
. In the other direction, we recover the original im-opfibration up to an isomorphism:
(\mathcal{Y}^{*})_{\otimes}\simeq\mathcal{Y}
, as the objects and morphisms in
\mathcal{Y}
that are not in
\mathcal{Y}^{*}
are first removed and then added with potentially new labels.
∎

We observe that Theorem
4.16
can be thought of as a kind of internalisation of the monoid on the opfibration. On the left-hand side of the equivalence, the monoid is an externally imposed structure, whereas on the right-hand side, the monoids are absorbed into the internal structure of the base and the total categories. In particular, given an im-opfibration
\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow\mathcal{X}
and an object
x\in\mathcal{O}b(\mathcal{X})
, we denote by
\otimes_{x}:\mathcal{Y}_{x}\times\mathcal{Y}_{x}\rightarrow\mathcal{Y}_{x}
the monoidal functor on the fibre
\mathcal{Y}_{x}
obtained from
\otimes_{f}
by setting
f=\mathsf{id}_{x}
in the above proof. We refer to this monoidal structure as
fibrewise
. It is precisely this internalisation that will make opfibrations with indexed monoids convenient to work with when defining the semantics of layered theories in Section
6.1
.

Combining Theorem
4.16
with Theorem
2.19
, we also have the following:

Corollary 4.17
.

Let
\mathcal{X}
be a small category. The category of split im-opfibrations with base
F_{\mathsf{im}}(\mathcal{X})
is equivalent to the category of strict
\mathcal{X}
-opindexed monoidal categories:

\mathbf{imOpFib}_{\mathsf{sp}}\left(F_{\mathsf{im}}(\mathcal{X})\right)\simeq\mathbf{OpIMonCat}_{\mathsf{st}}(\mathcal{X}).

The reader may wonder what happens in the general case, when the base of an im-opfibration is not freely generated. In such a case, each monoid in the base still induces some monoidal structure on the fibres, but now we are able to detect (or impose) properties of monoidal categories at the level of the base. For example, requiring the commutativity equation

=

to strictly hold in the split case would enforce the equation
a\otimes b=b\otimes a
in the corresponding fibre. In the general (non-split) case, this defines a natural isomorphism, i.e. a symmetric monoidal category. Thus, in order to properly exploit the additional equations in the base, one needs to move beyond the split (strict) setting. It is unclear whether an analogue of Theorem
4.16
holds in this case, as it is not obvious what the equations between the (pseudo)monoids on opfibrations should be. We leave exploring these developments to future work.

5
Deflations

We now wish to impose additional structure on a functor
\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow\mathcal{X}
so that it can be used as a model for layered theories with bidirectional functor boundaries. Proposition
2.32
suggests it should be a factorisation lifting, while Proposition
2.33
suggests it should somehow restrict to an opfibration, which would give the forward functor boundaries. We ensure that it also restricts to a fibration, giving the reverse functor boundary. We do this by freely adding right adjoints to the base category
\mathcal{X}
(Definition
5.1
), and by requiring that the adjoints lift to the total category (Definition
5.2
).

Let
\mathcal{X}
be a category. The collection of
zigzags
on
\mathcal{X}
is recursively defined as follows:

•

for every morphism
f:x\rightarrow y
in
\mathcal{X}
, the expressions
f:x\rightarrow y
and
\overline{f}:y\rightarrow x
are zigzags,

•

if
\varphi:x\rightarrow y
and
\gamma:y\rightarrow z
are zigzags, then so is
\varphi;\gamma:x\rightarrow z
.

In other words, a zigzag is a (bracketed) list of morphisms with possibly alternating directions; for example,
x\rightarrow y\leftarrow z\leftarrow w\rightarrow s
is a zigzag
x\rightarrow s
.

Definition 5.1

(Zigzag 2-category)
.

Given a small 1-category
\mathcal{X}
, the
zigzag 2-category

\mathsf{Zg}(\mathcal{X})
of
\mathcal{X}
is the strict 2-category whose 0-cells are the objects of
\mathcal{X}
and the 1-cells are given by the zigzags, subject to the following equations:

\displaystyle\overline{\mathsf{id}}_{x}

\displaystyle=\mathsf{id}_{x}

\displaystyle f;g

\displaystyle=fg

\displaystyle(\varphi;\gamma);\psi

\displaystyle=\varphi;(\gamma;\psi)

\displaystyle\overline{f};\overline{g}

\displaystyle=\overline{gf},

where
;
is used for composition of zigzags and concatenation is used for composition in
\mathcal{X}
. Given a morphism
f:x\rightarrow y
in
\mathcal{X}
, we have the following generating 2-cells:

\displaystyle\eta_{f}

\displaystyle:\mathsf{id}_{x}\rightarrow f;\overline{f}

\displaystyle\varepsilon_{f}

\displaystyle:\overline{f};f\rightarrow\mathsf{id}_{y},

subject to the zigzag equations defining an adjunction:

as well as the following coherence equations:

\displaystyle\eta_{\mathsf{id}_{x}}

\displaystyle=\mathsf{id}_{\mathsf{id}_{x}}

\displaystyle\eta_{f;h}

\displaystyle=\eta_{f};(\mathsf{id}_{f}*\eta_{h}*\mathsf{id}_{\overline{f}})

\displaystyle\varepsilon_{\mathsf{id}_{x}}

\displaystyle=\mathsf{id}_{\mathsf{id}_{x}}

\displaystyle\varepsilon_{f;h}

\displaystyle=(\mathsf{id}_{\overline{h}}*\varepsilon_{f}*\mathsf{id}_{h});\varepsilon_{h}.

For any category, there are the following identity-on-objects inclusions into its zigzag 2-category:

\displaystyle\mathcal{X}

\displaystyle\xhookrightarrow{\ \iota^{*}\ }\mathsf{Zg}(\mathcal{X}){}

\displaystyle\xhookleftarrow{\ \iota^{\circ}\ }\mathcal{X}^{op}

\displaystyle f

\displaystyle\longmapsto f\quad\ \overline{f}{}

\displaystyle\longmapsfrom f.

Definition 5.2

(Local retrofunctor)
.

Let
\mathcal{X}
and
\mathcal{Y}
be strict 2-categories. A
local retrofunctor

(p,\varphi):\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow\mathcal{X}
consists of a 1-functor
p:\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow\mathcal{X}
, and for all pairs of objects
a,b\in\mathcal{O}b(\mathcal{Y})
, a retrofunctor
(p,\varphi_{a,b}):\mathcal{Y}(a,b)\rightarrow\mathcal{X}(pa,pb)
whose function part is given by the action of
p
on morphisms, satisfying the following coherence equation for all
F:a\rightarrow b
,
F^{\prime}:b\rightarrow c
,
\alpha:pF\rightarrow g
,
\alpha^{\prime}:pF^{\prime}\rightarrow g^{\prime}
:

\varphi_{a,b}(F,\alpha)*\varphi_{b,c}(F^{\prime},\alpha^{\prime})=\varphi_{a,c}(F;F^{\prime},\alpha*\alpha^{\prime}).

We will now focus on local retrofunctors whose codomain is a zigzag 2-category, whose functor part is a factorisation lifting, together with a certain condition on the liftings of counits. This situation will play such a prominent role in the subsequent development that we give it a special name:
deflation
. We shall further introduce monoidal deflations, which will be used to give semantics to layered theories in Section
6.2
.

Let
(p,\varphi):\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow\mathsf{Zg}(\mathcal{X})
be a local retrofunctor such that
p:\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow\mathsf{Zg}(\mathcal{X})
is a factorisation lifting. A
lifting
of the opliftable pair
(a,f:x\rightarrow y)
such that
f\in\mathcal{X}
is any morphism
F:a\rightarrow b
obtained by decomposing the codomain of the 2-cell
\varphi_{a,a}\left(\mathsf{id}_{a},\eta_{f}\right)
into
F:a\rightarrow b
above
f:x\rightarrow y
and
\overline{F}:b\rightarrow a
above
\overline{f}:y\rightarrow x
:

Dually, we say that
\overline{F}:b\rightarrow a
is a
lifting
of the liftable pair
(\overline{f}:y\rightarrow x,a)
. In the context of deflations (which we about to define), the morphism of an opliftable pair will always be assumed to lie in
\iota^{*}\mathcal{X}
, and similarly, the morphism of a liftable pair will always be assumed to lie in
\iota^{\circ}\mathcal{X}
. While
a priori
the same pair can have many liftings, as we shall see imminently (Lemma
5.4
), in our situation of interest the liftings are essentially unique.

Definition 5.3

(Deflation)
.

Let
\mathcal{X}
be a 1-category and
\mathcal{Y}
be a strict 2-category. A
deflation
from
\mathcal{Y}
to
\mathcal{X}
is a local retrofunctor
(p,\varphi):\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow\mathsf{Zg}(\mathcal{X})
such that
p:\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow\mathsf{Zg}(\mathcal{X})
is a factorisation lifting, and for every lifting
F:a\rightarrow b
of an opliftable pair
(a,f:x\rightarrow y)
, the codomain of the 2-cell
\varphi_{b,b}\left(\overline{F};F,\varepsilon_{f}\right)
is
\mathsf{id}_{b}
:

We say that a deflation is
cloven
or
split
if the underlying factorisation lifting is.

Lemma 5.4
.

(p,\varphi):\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow\mathsf{Zg}(\mathcal{X})
be a deflation, and let
F:a\rightarrow b
be a lifting of an opliftable pair
(a,f:x\rightarrow y)
. Then for any morphism
F^{\prime}:a\rightarrow b^{\prime}
above
f
, there is a unique morphism
\alpha:b\rightarrow b^{\prime}
in the fibre
\mathcal{Y}_{y}
such that
F;\alpha=F^{\prime}
:

which simplifies to:

\displaystyle\phantom{=}\left(\varphi_{a,a}\left(\mathsf{id}_{a},\eta_{f}\right)*\mathsf{id}_{F^{\prime}}\right);\left(\mathsf{id}_{F}*\varphi_{b,b^{\prime}}\left(\overline{F};F^{\prime},\varepsilon_{f}\right)\right)

\displaystyle=\left(\varphi_{a,a}\left(\mathsf{id}_{a},\eta_{f}\right)*\varphi_{a,b^{\prime}}\left(F^{\prime},\mathsf{id}_{f}\right)\right);\left(\varphi_{a,b}\left(F,\mathsf{id}_{f}\right)*\varphi_{b,b^{\prime}}\left(\overline{F};F^{\prime},\varepsilon_{f}\right)\right)

\displaystyle=\varphi_{a,b^{\prime}}\left(F^{\prime},\eta_{f}*\mathsf{id}_{f}\right);\varphi_{a,b^{\prime}}\left(F;\overline{F};F^{\prime},\mathsf{id}_{f}*\varepsilon_{f}\right)

\displaystyle=\varphi_{a,b^{\prime}}\left(F^{\prime},\left(\eta_{f}*\mathsf{id}_{f}\right);\left(\mathsf{id}_{f}*\varepsilon_{f}\right)\right)

\displaystyle=\varphi_{a,b^{\prime}}\left(F^{\prime},\mathsf{id}_{f}\right)

\displaystyle=\mathsf{id}_{F^{\prime}},

which, in particular, implies that
F;\alpha=F^{\prime}
, as required.

For uniqueness, suppose that
\alpha^{\prime}:b\rightarrow b^{\prime}
is some 1-cell such that
F;\alpha^{\prime}=F^{\prime}
. We then compute

\displaystyle\varphi_{b,b^{\prime}}\left(\overline{F};F^{\prime},\varepsilon_{f}\right)

\displaystyle=\varphi_{b,b^{\prime}}\left(\overline{F};F;\alpha^{\prime},\varepsilon_{f}*\mathsf{id}_{\mathsf{id}_{y}}\right)

\displaystyle=\varphi_{b,b}\left(\overline{F};F,\varepsilon_{f}\right)*\varphi_{b,b^{\prime}}\left(\alpha^{\prime},\mathsf{id}_{\mathsf{id}_{y}}\right)

\displaystyle=\varphi_{b,b}\left(\overline{F};F,\varepsilon_{f}\right)*\mathsf{id}_{\alpha^{\prime}}.

Since the codomain of
\varphi_{b,b}\left(\overline{F};F,\varepsilon_{f}\right)
is
\mathsf{id}_{b}
, this, in particular, implies that
\alpha^{\prime}=\alpha
.
∎

Corollary 5.5
.

Let
(p,\varphi):\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow\mathsf{Zg}(\mathcal{X})
be a (split) deflation. Consider the restrictions of
p

\mathcal{Y}^{*}
\mathcal{Y}
\mathcal{X}
\mathsf{Zg}(\mathcal{X})
p
p^{*}
\mathcal{Y}^{\circ}
\mathcal{X}^{op}
p^{\circ}
\iota^{*}
\iota^{\circ}

to the wide subcategories
\mathcal{Y}^{*}
and
\mathcal{Y}^{\circ}
of
\mathcal{Y}
defined by
F\in\mathcal{Y}^{*}
if and only if
pF\in\iota^{*}\mathcal{X}
, and
F\in\mathcal{Y}^{\circ}
if and only if
pF\in\iota^{\circ}\mathcal{X}^{op}
. Then
p^{*}
is a (split) opfibration, and
p^{\circ}
is a (split) fibration.

Proof.

Lemma
5.4
establishes that
p^{*}
is a preopfibration. It is also a factorisation lifting by restricting the liftings of factorisations under
p
. Thus, by Corollary
2.34
,
p^{*}
is an opfibration. The argument establishing that
p^{\circ}
is a fibration is dual.
∎

and every 2-cell
\alpha:f\rightarrow g
we have

H\left(\varphi_{a,b}(F,\alpha)\right)=\varphi_{Ha,Hb}(HF,K\alpha).

A morphism of split deflations is additionally required to strictly preserve the chosen liftings of factorisations. We denote the category of deflations by
\mathbf{Defl}
, and the fixed base case by
\mathbf{Defl}(\mathcal{X})
. As before, we add the subscript
\mathsf{sp}
for the subcategories of split deflations.

Definition 5.7

(Minimal deflation)
.

We say that a deflation
(p,\varphi):\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow\mathsf{Zg}(\mathcal{X})
is
minimal
if the only non-identity 2-cells of
\mathcal{Y}
are the ones in the image of the retrofunctors
(p,\varphi_{a,b})
.

An equivalent way to define a minimal deflation would be to require
p
to be a 2-functor, and each retrofunctor
(p,\varphi_{a,b}):\mathcal{Y}(a,b)\rightarrow\mathcal{X}(pa,pb)
to be a
lens
, i.e. the lifted 2-cells should also be compatible with the action of
p
on 2-cells, not just the 1-cells. Minimal deflations are equivalent to (op)indexed categories (Theorem
5.9
).

Remark 5.8
.

The reason we wish to consider non-minimal deflations are many scenarios in which there are transformations between morphisms which are non-trivial, in the sense that they do not arise as liftings of the 2-cells in the base. For example, in
(
19
, 5.3)
we consider 2-cells that are semantics-preserving graph rewrites. Moreover, the syntax developed in Section
3
is sound and complete with respect to all deflations, not just the minimal ones. The general deflations, therefore, seem like a more natural semantic domain for interpreting layered theories.

Let us denote by
\mathbf{MinDefl}(\mathcal{X})
the full subcategory of
\mathbf{Defl}(\mathcal{X})
on minimal deflations.

Theorem 5.9
.

Let
\mathcal{X}
be a small category. There is an equivalence of categories between minimal deflations into
\mathcal{X}
and opindexed categories on
\mathcal{X}
:

\mathbf{MinDefl}(\mathcal{X})\simeq\mathbf{OpICat}(\mathcal{X}),

which restricts to split minimal deflations and strict functors
\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathbf{Cat}
.

Proof.

By Corollary
5.5
, each deflation restricts to an opfibration into
\mathcal{X}
. By Proposition
2.33
, the corresponding displayed category
\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathbf{Prof}
factors as
\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathbf{Cat}\xrightarrow{\blacktriangleleft}\mathbf{Prof}
, thus producing the desired indexed category. It is indeed a pseudofunctor by Proposition
2.32
, since the original deflation is a factorisation lifting.

Conversely, any opindexed category
D:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathbf{Cat}
extends to a normal pseudofunctor
\hat{D}:\mathsf{Zg}(\mathcal{X})\rightarrow\mathbf{Prof}
given by the action of the original functor
D
on the 0-cells, and by the following recursive definition on the 1-cells:

\displaystyle f

\displaystyle\mapsto(Df)^{\blacktriangleleft}

\displaystyle\overline{f}

\displaystyle\mapsto(Df)^{\vartriangleright}

\displaystyle\varphi;\gamma

\displaystyle\mapsto\hat{D}(\varphi);\hat{D}(\gamma),

where
;
on the right-hand side denotes the composition of profunctors. The generating 2-cells
\eta_{f}
and
\varepsilon_{f}
are, respectively, sent to the unit
\mathsf{id}_{Dx}\rightarrow(Df)^{\blacktriangleleft};(Df)^{\vartriangleright}
and the counit
(Df)^{\vartriangleright};(Df)^{\blacktriangleleft}\rightarrow\mathsf{id}_{Dy}
constructed in Proposition
2.25
. The collage of
\hat{D}
then gives the sought-after deflation
\coprod\hat{D}\rightarrow\mathsf{Zg}(\mathcal{X})
, with the 2-cells between two parallel morphisms
(f,F)
and
(g,G)
of type
(x,a)\rightarrow(y,b)
given by a 2-cell
\alpha:f\rightarrow g
in
\mathsf{Zg}(\mathcal{X})
such that
\hat{D}(\alpha)_{a,b}(F)=G
.

The equivalence on the 1-categorical part then follows by restricting the equivalence of Theorem
2.29
to deflations and indexed categories. Moreover, the 2-cells of the collage precisely recover the 2-cells of a minimal deflation, hence concluding the proof.
∎

5.1
Monoidal deflations

Next, we wish to incorporate monoidal structure into deflations. As for opfibrations, we do this via the means of indexed monoids. Recall that
F_{\mathsf{im}}(\mathcal{X})
denotes the free category with indexed monoids generated by a small category
\mathcal{X}
(Definition
4.11
). We denote the cartesian monoidal structure of
F_{\mathsf{im}}(\mathcal{X})
by
(\times,1)
. First, we observe that
\mathsf{Zg}(F_{\mathsf{im}}(\mathcal{X}))
can be given a monoidal structure as follows.

Proposition 5.10
.

Let
\mathcal{X}
be a small category with a cartesian monoidal structure
(\times,1)
. The zigzag 2-category
\mathsf{Zg}(\mathcal{X})
becomes a strict monoidal 2-category upon imposing the following additional equation for all
f:x\rightarrow y
and
g:z\rightarrow w
in
\mathcal{X}
:

(f\times\mathsf{id}_{w});\overline{(\mathsf{id}_{y}\times g)}=\overline{(g\times\mathsf{id}_{x})};(\mathsf{id}_{z}\times f).

Proof.

We define the monoidal functor
\times:\mathsf{Zg}(\mathcal{X})\times\mathsf{Zg}(\mathcal{X})\rightarrow\mathsf{Zg}(\mathcal{X})
on objects by the action of the product
\times
on
\mathcal{X}
, while for all
f:x\rightarrow y
and
g:z\rightarrow w
in
\mathcal{X}
, we define the product on the generating zigzags as follows, where on the right-hand side
\times
denotes the cartesian product of
\mathcal{X}
:

\displaystyle(f,g)

\displaystyle\mapsto f\times g,

\displaystyle(\overline{f},\overline{g})

\displaystyle\mapsto\overline{f\times g},

\displaystyle(f,\overline{g})

\displaystyle\mapsto(f\times\mathsf{id}_{w});\overline{(\mathsf{id}_{y}\times g)},

\displaystyle(\overline{f},g)

\displaystyle\mapsto\overline{(f\times\mathsf{id}_{z})};(\mathsf{id}_{x}\times g).

Finally, on the generating 2-cells we stipulate as follows, where, as before,
f:x\rightarrow y
and
g:z\rightarrow w
are in
\mathcal{X}
and
\times
on the right-hand side denotes the cartesian product of
\mathcal{X}
:

\displaystyle\eta_{f}\times\eta_{g}

\displaystyle\coloneq\eta_{f\times g},

\displaystyle\varepsilon_{f}\times\varepsilon_{g}

\displaystyle\coloneq\varepsilon_{f\times g},

\displaystyle\eta_{f}\times\varepsilon_{g}

\displaystyle\coloneq\varepsilon_{\mathsf{id}_{x}\times g};\eta_{f\times\mathsf{id}_{w}},

\displaystyle\varepsilon_{f}\times\eta_{g}

\displaystyle\coloneq\varepsilon_{f\times\mathsf{id}_{z}};\eta_{\mathsf{id}_{y}\times g}.

The monoidal unit is given by that of
\mathcal{X}
, i.e. by
1
.
∎

Whenever we write
\mathsf{Zg}(F_{\mathsf{im}}(\mathcal{X}))
, we assume that it has the monoidal structure as described in Proposition
5.10
, which we also denote by
(\times,1)
. Note that, despite notation, this monoidal structure is
not
cartesian monoidal.

Definition 5.11

(Monoidal deflation)
.

A
monoidal deflation
is a deflation
(p,\varphi):\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow\mathsf{Zg}(F_{\mathsf{im}}(\mathcal{X}))
such that
\mathcal{Y}
is a strict monoidal 2-category with the monoidal structure
(\otimes,I)
such that
p
strictly preserves and reflects the monoidal structure:

•

for all
a\in\mathcal{O}b(\mathcal{Y})
, we have
p(a)=1
if and only if
a=I
,

•

for all
F,G\in\mathcal{Y}
, we have
p(F\otimes G)=pF\times pG
,

•

for all
H\in\mathcal{Y}
and
f,g\in\mathsf{Zg}(F_{\mathsf{im}}(\mathcal{X}))
, if
pH=f\times g
, then there are
F,G\in\mathcal{Y}
with
pF=f
,
pG=g
and
F\otimes G=H
,

and the following additional equation holds for all 1-cells
F:a\rightarrow b
and
G:c\rightarrow d
in
\mathcal{Y}
that, respectively, are above the domains of the 2-cells
\alpha
and
\beta
in
\mathsf{Zg}(F_{\mathsf{im}}(\mathcal{X}))
:

\varphi_{a\otimes c,b\otimes d}(F\otimes G,\alpha\times\beta)=\varphi_{a,b}(F,\alpha)\otimes\varphi_{c,d}(G,\beta).

Note that, unlike in the definition of im-opfibrations (Definition
4.13
), we do not require that the monoidal product on the total category of a monoidal deflation sends liftings to liftings in any sense. This, however, follows from other requirements, as we record in the following proposition.

Proposition 5.12
.

Let
(p,\varphi):\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow\mathsf{Zg}(F_{\mathsf{im}}(\mathcal{X}))
be a monoidal deflation. Let
F:a\rightarrow b
and
G:c\rightarrow d
, respectively, be liftings of opliftable pairs
(a,f:x\rightarrow y)
and
(c,g:z\rightarrow w)
. Then
F\otimes G
is a lifting of
(a\otimes c,f\times g)
.

Proof.

The lifting of
(a\otimes c,f\times g)
is defined by factorising the codomain of the following 2-cell:

\displaystyle\varphi_{a\otimes c,a\otimes c}(\mathsf{id}_{a\otimes c},\eta_{f\times g})

\displaystyle=\varphi_{a\otimes c,a\otimes c}(\mathsf{id}_{a}\otimes\mathsf{id}_{c},\eta_{f}\times\eta_{g})

\displaystyle=\varphi_{a,a}(\mathsf{id}_{a},\eta_{f})\otimes\varphi_{c,c}(\mathsf{id}_{c},\eta_{g}),

which is therefore equal to
(F;\overline{F})\otimes(G;\overline{G})=(F\otimes G);(\overline{F};\overline{G})
. Thus,
F\otimes G
is indeed a lifting.
∎

Since liftings in deflations are unique up to an isomorphism, Proposition
5.12
implies that in monoidal deflations liftings of products are given by products of liftings. We say that a monoidal deflation is
split
if the underlying deflation is split, and the chosen liftings of products are the products of chosen liftings.

A morphism of monoidal deflations is given by a morphism of deflations
(H,K)
such that
H
is additionally a strict monoidal functor. We denote the various categories of monoidal deflations by
\mathbf{MonDefl}
.

The following lemma establishes a tight link between monoidal deflations and opfibrations with indexed monoids (Definition
4.13
).

Lemma 5.13
.

Let
(p,\varphi):\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow\mathsf{Zg}(F_{\mathsf{im}}(\mathcal{X}))
be a split deflation. If
p
is monoidal, then the opfibration
p^{*}
obtained by restriction

\mathcal{Y}^{*}
\mathcal{Y}
F_{\mathsf{im}}(\mathcal{X})
\mathsf{Zg}(F_{\mathsf{im}}(\mathcal{X}))
p
p^{*}

has indexed monoids. Moreover, if
p
is minimal, then the converse also holds: if the restriction
p^{*}
has indexed monoids, then the deflation
p
is monoidal.

Proof.

First, suppose that the (not necessarily minimal) deflation
p
is monoidal. Given objects
a,b\in\mathcal{O}b(\mathcal{Y})
with
pa=x
, define the counit
C_{a}:a\rightarrow 1
as the opcartesian lifting of the counit
(a,x\rightarrow 1)
, and the maps

a
a^{\prime}
a^{\prime\prime}
a
b
\hat{b}
\hat{a}
S_{a,b}

as the opcartesian liftings of the diagonal and the symmetry, respectively. Compositionality of the opcartesian liftings, together with preservation and reflection of the monoidal structure, then implies that
a^{\prime}=a^{\prime\prime}=\hat{a}
and
b=\hat{b}
, so that we may define the above maps as the diagonal and the symmetry. The equations for symmetries and uniform comonoids then follow, once again by compositionality of the opcartesian liftings. Thus,
\mathcal{Y}^{*}
is cartesian monoidal by Proposition
4.2
, and the cartesian monoidal structure is preserved and reflected by assumption, establishing that
p^{*}
has indexed monoids.

For the (partial) converse, suppose that
p
is minimal and that
p^{*}
has indexed monoids. Let us denote by
\times^{*}:\mathcal{Y}^{*}\times\mathcal{Y}^{*}\rightarrow\mathcal{Y}^{*}
the cartesian product functor on
\mathcal{Y}^{*}
. We define the monoidal functor
\otimes:\mathcal{Y}\times\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow\mathcal{Y}
on objects by the action of
\times^{*}
. For defining
\otimes
on morphisms, observe that Lemma
5.4
(and its dual) implies that the morphisms in
\mathcal{Y}
are generated by morphisms of the following form:

\alpha;F;\beta;\overline{G},

where
F
is a lifting of some
f\in\iota^{*}(\mathcal{X})
and
\overline{G}
is a lifting of some
\overline{g}\in\iota^{\circ}(\mathcal{X}^{op})
, while
\alpha
and
\beta
are in the fibres of the domain and codomain of
f
. Absorbing
\alpha
and
\beta
into
F
, we conclude that the morphisms of
\mathcal{Y}
are generated by morphisms of the form
F;\overline{G}
, where
F\in\mathcal{Y}^{*}
and
G
is, as before, a lifting of some
\overline{g}\in\iota^{\circ}(\mathcal{X}^{op})
. Hence, it suffices to define the monoidal product on these two classes of morphisms. Hence let
F,F^{\prime}\in\mathcal{Y}^{*}
and let
\overline{G},\overline{G^{\prime}}
lifting of liftable pairs, with
F:a\rightarrow b
and
\overline{G}:c\rightarrow d
. We define

\displaystyle F\otimes F^{\prime}

\displaystyle\coloneq F\times^{*}F^{\prime},

\displaystyle F\otimes\overline{G}

\displaystyle\coloneq(F\times^{*}\mathsf{id}_{c});\overline{(\mathsf{id}_{b}\times^{*}G)},

\displaystyle\overline{G}\otimes\overline{G^{\prime}}

\displaystyle\coloneq\overline{G\times^{*}G^{\prime}},

\displaystyle\overline{G}\otimes F

\displaystyle\coloneq\overline{(G\times^{*}\mathsf{id}_{a})};(\mathsf{id}_{d}\times^{*}F).

The monoidal unit is given by that of
\mathcal{Y}^{*}
, and this monoidal structure is preserved and reflected by
p
. It remains to define
\otimes
on the 2-cells. Since the deflation
p
is minimal, it suffices to define
\otimes
on the liftings of the 2-cells in
\mathsf{Zg}(F_{\mathsf{im}}(\mathcal{X}))
, which we do as follows, where
\alpha
and
\beta
are any 2-cells in
\mathsf{Zg}(F_{\mathsf{im}}(\mathcal{X}))
, while
F:a\rightarrow b
and
G:c\rightarrow d
are above their domains:

\varphi_{a,b}(F,\alpha)\otimes\varphi_{c,d}(G,\beta)\coloneq\varphi_{a\times^{*}c,b\times^{*}d}(F\otimes G,\alpha\times\beta).

∎

Note that Lemma
5.13
implies that every split monoidal deflation has a fibrewise monoidal structure induced by the fibrewise monoidal structure of the split opfibration with indexed monoids obtained by restriction. Moreover, this fibrewise monoidal structure coincides with the fibrewise monoidal structure induced by the split fibration with indexed comonoids obtained by restriction (Corollary
5.5
). As for im-opfibrations, we denote the fibrewise monoidal structure in the fibre of
x
by
\otimes_{x}
.

The construction in the proof of Lemma
5.13
establishes the following theorem, linking monoidal deflations and opfibrations with indexed monoids. By results of Section
4.2
(specifically Theorem
4.16
and Corollary
4.17
), minimal monoidal deflations are equivalent to opfibrations with a monoid and strict opindexed monoidal categories (i.e. functors)
\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathbf{MonCat}_{\mathsf{st}}
.

Theorem 5.14
.

Let
\mathcal{X}
be a small category. The categories of minimal split monoidal deflations into
\mathcal{X}
and split im-opfibrations into
F_{\mathsf{im}}(\mathcal{X})
are equivalent:

\mathbf{MinMonDefl}_{\mathsf{sp}}(\mathcal{X})\simeq\mathbf{imOpFib}_{\mathsf{sp}}(F_{\mathsf{im}}(\mathcal{X})).

Proof.

Given a minimal split monoidal deflation
(p,\varphi):\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow\mathcal{\mathsf{Zg}}(F_{\mathsf{im}}(X))
, the corresponding split im-opfibration is given by the restriction
p^{*}:\mathcal{Y}^{*}\rightarrow F_{\mathsf{im}}(\mathcal{X})
.

Conversely, given a split im-opfibration
p:\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow F_{\mathsf{im}}(\mathcal{X})
, we extend it to a split deflation
(\hat{p},\varphi):\hat{\mathcal{Y}}\rightarrow\mathcal{\mathsf{Zg}}(F_{\mathsf{im}}(X))
as follows. The category
\hat{\mathcal{Y}}
has the same objects as
\mathcal{Y}
, while the morphisms are defined as:

•

each morphism of
\mathcal{Y}
is a morphism of
\hat{\mathcal{Y}}
, so that
\mathcal{Y}
is a subcategory of
\hat{\mathcal{Y}}
,

•

for each opcartesian
F\in\mathcal{Y}
, we add the morphism
\overline{F}
in the opposite direction and let
p\overline{F}\coloneq\overline{pF}
,

•

we impose the following equations on the morphisms:
\overline{\mathsf{id}_{a}}=\mathsf{id}_{a}
and
\overline{F};\overline{G}=\overline{G;F}
.

The 2-cells are generated by adding exactly those 2-cells required by the local retrofunctor, i.e. for every 2-cell
\alpha
in
F_{\mathsf{im}}(\mathcal{X})
and every
F:a\rightarrow b
in
\hat{\mathcal{Y}}
above the domain of
\alpha
we add a generating 2-cell
\varphi_{a,b}(F,\alpha)
, subject to the equations of a deflation. Now,
(\hat{p},\varphi)
is a minimal split deflation, whose restriction is the split im-opfibration
p
we started with. Lemma
5.13
guarantees that
(\hat{p},\varphi)
is monoidal.
∎

In light of Theorem
5.14
, one might ask why go through all the developments of the current section just to obtain something we already defined in the previous section? Why not directly work with im-opfibrations and be content? The answer is twofold. First, presenting an (op)indexed monoidal category (equivalently, an im-opfibration) as a monoidal deflation explicitly introduces the functor boundaries in both directions, displaying the categories and the functors involved in a highly modular way. This makes deflations ideal for a purely syntactic treatment, which is the subject of the next section. Second, dropping the requirement of minimality, we do obtain a genuine generalisation of (op)indexed monoidal categories: the axiomatisation of the next section is sound and complete with respect to all monoidal deflations, not merely the minimal ones.

6
Semantics of layered theories

In this final section, we define the models of opfibrational, fibrational and deflation theories in full generality. In each case, we construct a free-forgetful adjunction with the category of models: opfibrations with indexed monoids, fibrations with indexed monoids and monoidal deflations.

6.1
(Op)fibrational models

Here we consider models of layered theories consisting of a split im-opfibration
\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow F_{\mathsf{im}}(\mathcal{X})
(see section
4.2
) together with an interpretation of all types, terms and 2-terms of the theory.

Definition 6.1

(Opfibrational model of a layered signature)
.

An
opfibrational model
of a layered signature
(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathcal{M}_{\omega})
is a split im-opfibration
p:\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow F_{\mathsf{im}}(\mathcal{X})
, together with the following data:

•

a function
i:\Omega\rightarrow\mathcal{O}b(\mathcal{X})
,

•

for every
\omega,\tau\in\Omega
, a function
i_{\omega,\tau}:\mathcal{F}(\omega,\tau)\rightarrow\mathcal{X}(i\omega,i\tau)
,

•

for every
\omega\in\Omega
, a function
i^{\omega}:C_{\omega}\rightarrow\mathcal{O}b(\mathcal{Y}_{i\omega})
,

•

for every
\omega\in\Omega
and all
a,b\in C_{\omega}^{*}
, a function
i^{\omega}_{a,b}:\Sigma_{\omega}(a,b)\rightarrow\mathcal{Y}_{i\omega}\left(\left(i^{\omega}\right)^{*}a,\left(i^{\omega}\right)^{*}b\right)
,

where
(i^{\omega})^{*}:C_{\omega}^{*}\rightarrow\mathcal{O}b(\mathcal{Y}_{i\omega})
is defined by extending
i^{\omega}
to the fibrewise monoidal structure of
p
.

Note that the last two bullet points imply that for each
\omega\in\Omega
, the fibre
\mathcal{Y}_{i\omega}
is a model of the monoidal signature
\mathcal{M}_{\omega}
in the sense of Definition
2.46
. We denote a model of
(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathcal{M}_{\omega})
by
(p,i)
.

Given an opfibrational model
(p:\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow F_{\mathsf{im}}(\mathcal{X}),i)
of
\mathcal{L}=(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathcal{M}_{\omega})
, it induces a function
i:\texttt{Type}_{\mathcal{L}}\rightarrow\mathcal{O}b(\mathcal{Y})
recursively defined as follows:

\displaystyle\varepsilon:\varepsilon

\displaystyle\mapsto 1,

\displaystyle\varepsilon:\omega

\displaystyle\mapsto I_{i\omega}

\displaystyle a:\omega

\displaystyle\mapsto i^{\omega}(a)

\displaystyle f(A):\tau

\displaystyle\mapsto i_{\omega,\tau}(f)^{*}\left(i(A:\omega)\right)

\displaystyle AB:\omega

\displaystyle\mapsto i(A:\omega)\otimes_{i\omega}i(B:\omega),

\displaystyle T,S

\displaystyle\mapsto i(T)\times i(S),

where
i_{\omega,\tau}(f)^{*}:\mathcal{Y}_{i\omega}\rightarrow\mathcal{Y}_{i\tau}
is the reindexing functor induced by
i_{\omega,\tau}(f):i\omega\rightarrow i\tau
.

Likewise, the same opfibrational model further induces the function
i:\texttt{Term}^{1}_{\mathcal{L}}\rightarrow\mathcal{Y}
form the basic (Figure
2
), symmetry (Definition
3.18
) and opfibrational (Figure
5
) terms as follows:

\displaystyle x;y

\displaystyle\mapsto i(x);i(y)

\displaystyle x\otimes y

\displaystyle\mapsto i(x)\times i(y),

where
i_{\omega,\tau}(f)^{*}:\mathcal{Y}_{i\omega}\rightarrow\mathcal{Y}_{i\tau}
is the reindexing functor induced by
i_{\omega,\tau}(f):i\omega\rightarrow i\tau
, and

i_{\omega,\tau}(f)_{i(A:\omega)}:i(A:\omega)\rightarrow i(f(A):\tau)

is the opcartesian lifting of the opliftable pair
\left(i(A:\omega),i_{\omega,\tau}(f):i\omega\rightarrow i\tau\right)
.

Definition 6.2
.

A
model of an opfibrational layered theory
with signature
\mathcal{L}
is an opfibrational model
(p,i)
of
\mathcal{L}
such that the induced functions
i:\texttt{Type}_{\mathcal{L}}\rightarrow\mathcal{O}b(\mathcal{Y})
and
i:\texttt{Term}^{1}_{\mathcal{L}}\rightarrow\mathcal{Y}
preserve the 0- and the 1-equations, respectively.

Proposition 6.3
.

Any opfibrational model of a layered signature preserves the structural opfibrational equations (Definition
3.22
).

Proof.

The structural 0-equations (Definition
3.15
) are preserved by associativity and unitality of the monoids, and by the fact that the reindexing functors preserve the monoidal multiplication and units.

The structural 1-equations (Definition
3.16
) are preserved since
\mathcal{Y}
is (cartesian) monoidal, each fibre
\mathcal{Y}_{i\omega}
is a monoidal category, and
\otimes_{x}:\mathcal{Y}_{x}\times\mathcal{Y}_{x}\rightarrow\mathcal{Y}_{x}
is a functor.

The structural 1-equations in Figure
3
are preserved since the reindexing functors between the fibres are strictly functorial and monoidal.

The symmetry equations are preserved since
\mathcal{Y}
is cartesian monoidal, hence in particular symmetric monoidal. Likewise, the equations of uniform comonoids are preserved since
\mathcal{Y}
is cartesian monoidal.

The equations in Figure
6
are preserved by lifting the corresponding equations from the base category.

Preservation of the equations in Figure
7
is somewhat less immediate. For the first equation, assuming the sorts
x:(A:\omega\mid B:\omega)
and
f\in\mathcal{F}(\omega,\tau)
we have to show that

i(x);i_{\omega,\tau}(f)_{i(B:\omega)}=i_{\omega,\tau}(f)_{i(A:\omega)};i_{\omega,\tau}(f)^{*}(i(x)),

which holds by the definition of
i_{\omega,\tau}(f)^{*}(i(x))
: it is the unique map induced by the lifting property of the opcartesian map
i_{\omega,\tau}(f)_{i(A:\omega)}
that makes the square

i(A:\omega)
i(B:\omega)
i(f(A):\tau)
i(f(B):\tau)
i(x)
i_{\omega,\tau}(f)_{i(A:\omega)}
i_{\omega,\tau}(f)_{i(B:\omega)}
i_{\omega,\tau}(f)^{*}(i(x))

commute. The remaining two equations in Figure
6
are preserved by Theorem
4.16
.
∎

Definition 6.4
.

The category of
models of opfibrational theories

\mathbf{OpFThMod}
has as objects tuples
(\mathcal{T},p,i)
of an opfibrational theory
\mathcal{T}
and its model
p:\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow F_{\mathsf{im}}(\mathcal{X})
(with the corresponding family of interpretation functions
i
). A morphism

(F,P,Q):(\mathcal{T},p:\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow\mathcal{X},i)\rightarrow(\mathcal{K},q:\mathcal{Y}^{\prime}\rightarrow\mathcal{X}^{\prime},j)

is given by a morphism of opfibrational theories
F:\mathcal{T}\rightarrow\mathcal{K}
together with a morphism of im-opfibrations
(P,Q):p\rightarrow q
such that the diagrams below commute, where we assume that the layered signature of
\mathcal{T}
is
(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathcal{M}_{\omega})
and the layered signature of
\mathcal{K}
is
(\Psi,\mathcal{G},\mathcal{M}_{\psi})
:

Note that the bottom diagrams say that for every
\omega\in\Omega
, the restriction of
P:\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow\mathcal{Y}^{\prime}
to the fibre
P_{i\omega}:\mathcal{Y}_{i\omega}\rightarrow\mathcal{Y}^{\prime}_{jF(\omega)}
makes
(F^{\omega},P_{i\omega})
into a morphism in
\mathbf{MMod}
.

We denote the full subcategory of
\mathbf{OpFThMod}
defined by the theories whose sets of equations are empty by
\mathbf{OpFMod}
, and call it the category of
opfibrational models of layered signatures
, since models of empty theories are in one-to-one correspondence with models of signatures. We summarise the relationship between opfibrational theories, models and layered signatures in the following proposition (cf. Proposition
2.49
).

Proposition 6.5
.

The vertical forgetful functors in the diagram below are fibrations, while the horizontal forgetful functors form a morphism of fibrations:

Moreover, the objects in the fibre
\mathbf{OpFMod}(\mathcal{L})
are precisely the opfibrational models of the layered signature
\mathcal{L}
, and the objects in the fibre
\mathbf{OpFThMod}(\mathcal{T})
are precisely the models of the opfibrational theory
\mathcal{T}
.

Similarly to Proposition
2.49
, we note that
\mathbf{OpFTh}\rightarrow\mathbf{LSgn}
is also a fibration, while the functor
\mathbf{OpFThMod}\rightarrow\mathbf{OpFMod}
fails to be a fibration.

We conclude the discussion of opfibrational models by constructing free models generated by opfibrational theories, i.e. by constructing the left adjoint to the vertical forgetful functors of Proposition
6.5
. We first define the total and the base categories generated by a theory and construct the im-opfibration between them.

Definition 6.6

(Total category generated by an opfibrational theory)
.

Let
\mathcal{T}=(\mathcal{L},E^{0},E^{1})
be an opfibrational theory. The
total category

T(\mathcal{T})
generated by
\mathcal{T}
has the equivalence classes of types
\texttt{Type}_{\mathcal{L}}
under the type congruence generated by
E^{0}\cup S^{0}
as objects, and the morphisms are the equivalence classes of terms
\texttt{Term}^{1}_{\mathcal{L}}
under the term congruence generated by
E^{1}\cup S_{\mathsf{opf}}^{1}
.

Definition 6.7

(Base category generated by a layered signature)
.

Let
\mathcal{L}=(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathcal{M}_{\omega})
be a layered signature. The
base category

B(\mathcal{L})
generated by
\mathcal{L}
is the free category with indexed monoids generated by
(\Omega,\mathcal{F})
viewed as a monoidal signature.

Given an opfibrational theory
\mathcal{T}=(\mathcal{L},E^{0},E^{1})
with
\mathcal{L}=(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathcal{M}_{\omega})
, define the functor
p_{\mathcal{T}}:T(\mathcal{T})\rightarrow B(\mathcal{L})
on internal types by
A:\omega\mapsto\omega
, on all types by extension to products, and by action on the generating terms as follows, where
x:(A:\omega\mid B:\omega)
is any internal term:

Proposition 6.8
.

For any opfibrational theory
\mathcal{T}
with the layered signature
\mathcal{L}
, the functor
p_{\mathcal{T}}:T(\mathcal{T})\rightarrow B(\mathcal{L})
is a split im-opfibration.

Proof.

We observe that the opcartesian morphisms in
T(\mathcal{T})
are given by those terms that are equal to a term with no non-trivial internal structure. More precisely, a morphism is opcartesian if and only if the equivalence class contains a term whose construction does not involve the rule
. We now observe that if we set the internal term
x
to be the identity term in the definition of
p_{\mathcal{T}}:T(\mathcal{T})\rightarrow B(\mathcal{L})
, then for any type
S
and a generating morphism
f:p_{\mathcal{T}}(S)\rightarrow\omega
, there is a unique term
\hat{f}:S\rightarrow K
in
T(\mathcal{T})
with
M_{\mathcal{T}}\left(\hat{f}\right)=f
, which is moreover opcartesian. Extending this to all morphisms gives the split opfibration structure of
p_{\mathcal{T}}
, which is, moreover, consistent with the (cartesian) monoidal structure of
T(\mathcal{T})
. Finally, the opfibration
p_{\mathcal{T}}
has indexed monoids by construction.
∎

Corollary 6.9
.

Any opfibrational theory
\mathcal{T}=(\mathcal{L},E^{0},E^{1})
gives rise to the opfibrational model
\left(p_{\mathcal{T}}:T(\mathcal{T})\rightarrow B(\mathcal{L}),i\right)
, whose interpretation functions
i
are given by:

\displaystyle i(\omega)

\displaystyle=\omega,

\displaystyle i_{\omega,\tau}(f)

\displaystyle=f,

\displaystyle i^{\omega}(a)

\displaystyle=a:\omega,

\displaystyle i^{\omega}_{A,B}(\sigma)

\displaystyle=\sigma:(A:\omega\mid B:\omega).

We have finally arrived to the main theorem about opfibrational theories.

Theorem 6.10
.

The construction of opfibrational models from opfibrational theories extends to a functor
\mathbf{OpFTh}\rightarrow\mathbf{OpFThMod}
, which is moreover the left adjoint to the forgetful functor.

Proof.

Any morphism of opfibrational theories
F:\mathcal{T}\rightarrow\mathcal{K}
recursively extends to types and terms, as shown in Section
3
, giving the functor between the total categories
T(\mathcal{T})\rightarrow T(\mathcal{K})
. The induced functor between the base categories
B(\mathcal{T})\rightarrow B(\mathcal{K})
is given by extending the action of
F
on the layers and the generators to a morphism of indexed monoids. This gives a morphism of im-opfibrations.

By Proposition
6.3
, the term model of
\mathcal{T}
is the initial object of the fibre
\mathbf{OpFThMod}(\mathcal{T})
. Moreover, any morphism out of the term model of
\mathcal{T}
into any model of
\mathcal{K}
factors through the term model of
\mathcal{K}
, thus exhibiting the desired adjunction.
∎

Corollary 6.11
.

For any opfibrational theory
\mathcal{T}
and layered signature
\mathcal{L}
, we have the following equivalences:

\displaystyle\mathbf{OpFThMod}(\mathcal{T})

\displaystyle\simeq\left.\raisebox{1.02228pt}{$F(\mathcal{T})$}\middle/\raisebox{-1.02228pt}{$\mathbf{MonOpFib}_{\mathsf{sp}}$}\right.,

\displaystyle\mathbf{OpFMod}(\mathcal{L})

\displaystyle\simeq\left.\raisebox{1.02228pt}{$F(\mathcal{L})$}\middle/\raisebox{-1.02228pt}{$\mathbf{MonOpFib}_{\mathsf{sp}}$}\right..

The class of models characterised by fibrational theories are
fibrations with indexed comonoids

\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow F_{\mathsf{im}}(\mathcal{X})^{op}
obtained by appropriately dualising Definition
4.13
. The free fibrational models are obtained by imposing the structural fibrational equations (Definition
3.23
) on the fibrational terms in Figure
8
.

6.2
Deflational models

As anticipated, the deflational models are given by split monoidal deflations (Definition
5.11
).

Definition 6.12

(Deflational model)
.

A
deflational model
of a layered signature
(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathcal{M}_{\omega})
is a split monoidal deflation
(p,\varphi):\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow\mathsf{Zg}(F_{\mathsf{im}}(\mathcal{X}))
together with the following data:

•

a function
i:\Omega\rightarrow\mathcal{O}b(\mathcal{X})
,

•

for every
\omega,\tau\in\Omega
, a function
i_{\omega,\tau}:\mathcal{F}(\omega,\tau)\rightarrow\mathcal{X}(i\omega,i\tau)
,

•

for every
\omega\in\Omega
, a function
i^{\omega}:C_{\omega}\rightarrow\mathcal{O}b(\mathcal{Y}_{i\omega})
,

•

for every
\omega\in\Omega
and all
a,b\in C_{\omega}^{*}
, a function
i^{\omega}_{a,b}:\Sigma_{\omega}(a,b)\rightarrow\mathcal{Y}_{i\omega}\left(\left(i^{\omega}\right)^{*}a,\left(i^{\omega}\right)^{*}b\right)
,
where
(i^{\omega})^{*}:C_{\omega}^{*}\rightarrow\mathcal{O}b(\mathcal{Y}_{i\omega})
is defined by extending
i^{\omega}
to the fibrewise monoidal structure of
p
.

Note that a deflational model on
(p,\varphi):\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow\mathsf{Zg}(F_{\mathsf{im}}(\mathcal{X}))
is at the same time an opfibrational model on the restriction
p^{*}:\mathcal{Y}^{*}\rightarrow F_{\mathsf{im}}(\mathcal{X})

and
a fibrational model on the restriction
p^{\circ}:\mathcal{Y}^{\circ}\rightarrow F_{\mathsf{im}}(\mathcal{X})^{op}
. We denote a model of
(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathcal{M}_{\omega})
by
(p,\varphi,i)
.

Since any deflational model
(p,\varphi,i)
of
\mathcal{L}
restricts to an opfibrational model, it induces the function
i:\texttt{Type}_{\mathcal{L}}\rightarrow\mathcal{O}b(\mathcal{Y})
, as
\mathcal{Y}^{*}
and
\mathcal{Y}
have the same objects. Moreover, this function is equal to the function induced by the restricted fibrational model.

The opfibrational restriction
p^{*}:\mathcal{Y}^{*}\rightarrow F_{\mathsf{im}}(\mathcal{X})
is likewise used to obtain the function from the basic (Figure
2
), symmetry (Definition
3.18
) and opfibrational (Figure
5
) terms into
\mathcal{Y}^{*}
, as described in Section
6.1
. In order to obtain the function
i:\texttt{Term}_{\mathcal{L}}^{1}\rightarrow\mathcal{Y}
, it remains to interpret the fibrational terms (Figure
8
), as well as to extend the interpretation to composite terms. Hence, let each fibrational term be interpreted as the dual of the corresponding opfibrational term, while the composition and product are interpreted as composition and the (global) monoidal product in
\mathcal{Y}
. Explicitly, we stipulate:

\vartriangleright_{f}

\displaystyle\mapsto\overline{i_{\omega,\tau}(f)_{i(A:\omega)}}

\displaystyle\begin{split}x;y&\mapsto i(x);i(y)\\

Definition 6.13
.

A
model of a deflational layered theory

(\mathcal{L},E^{0},E^{1},\eta,E^{2})
consists of: (1) a deflational model
(p,\varphi,i)
of
\mathcal{L}
(Definition
6.12
) such that the induced functions
i:\texttt{Type}_{\mathcal{L}}\rightarrow\mathcal{O}b(\mathcal{Y})
and
i:\texttt{Term}_{\mathcal{L}}^{1}\rightarrow\mathcal{Y}_{1}
preserve
E^{0}
and
E^{1}
, and (2) for each parallel pair of terms
(x,y)\in P^{1}_{\mathcal{L}}
with sort
(T\mid S)
a function

i_{x,y}:\eta(x,y)\sqcup\eta_{\mathsf{str}}(x,y)\rightarrow\mathcal{Y}_{2}\left(i(x),i(y)\right)

from the generating 2-cells into the 2-cells
i(x)\rightarrow i(y)
, such that the structural 2-cells are mapped to the following 2-cells returned by the retrofunctor:

\displaystyle\eta_{x}\mapsto\varphi_{i(T),i(T)}\left(\mathsf{id}_{i(T)},\eta_{i(x)}\right)

\displaystyle\varepsilon_{x}\mapsto\varphi_{i(S),i(S)}\left(i(\bar{x});i(x),\varepsilon_{i(x)}\right),

and the function
i:\texttt{Term}^{2}_{\mathcal{L}}\rightarrow\mathcal{Y}_{2}
on all 2-terms (Definition
3.9
) recursively obtained from
\eta\sqcup\eta_{\mathsf{str}}
preserves
E^{2}
.

Proposition 6.14
.

Any deflational model of a deflational layered theory preserves the structural deflational equations (Definition
3.26
).

Proof.

The structural opfibrational and fibrational equations are preserved by Proposition
6.3
(and its dual). The 2-equations are preserved since the local retrofunctor preserves both vertical and composition, and therefore equations between 2-cells.
∎

Definition 6.15
.

The category of
models of deflational theories

\mathbf{DeflThMod}
has as objects tuples
(\mathcal{T},p,\varphi,i)
of a deflational theory
\mathcal{T}
and its model
(p,\varphi):\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow\mathsf{Zg}(F_{\mathsf{im}}(\mathcal{X}))
with the family of interpretation functions
i
. A morphism

(F,F^{2},P,Q):(\mathcal{T},p,\varphi,i)\rightarrow(\mathcal{K},q,\rho,j),

is given by a morphism of deflational theories
(F,F^{2}):\mathcal{T}\rightarrow\mathcal{K}
together with a morphism of monoidal deflations
(P,Q):(p,\varphi)\rightarrow(q,\rho)
such that the diagrams of Definition
6.4
as well as the diagrams below commute, where
(p,\varphi):\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow\mathsf{Zg}(F_{\mathsf{im}}(\mathcal{X}))
and
(q,\rho):\mathcal{Y}^{\prime}\rightarrow\mathsf{Zg}(F_{\mathsf{im}}(\mathcal{X}^{\prime}))
, and we write
\eta_{\mathcal{T}}
and
\eta_{\mathcal{K}}
for the choice of 2-cells in
\mathcal{T}
and
\mathcal{K}
, and
(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathcal{M}_{\omega})
for the layered signature of
\mathcal{T}
and
(\Psi,\mathcal{G},\mathcal{M}_{\psi})
for the layered signature of
\mathcal{K}
:

\mathbf{DeflMod}(\mathcal{L})
are precisely the deflational models of the layered signature
\mathcal{L}

As in Propositions
2.49
and
6.5
, we note that
\mathbf{DeflTh}\rightarrow\mathbf{LSgn}
is also a fibration, while the functor
\mathbf{DeflThMod}\rightarrow\mathbf{DeflMod}
fails to be a fibration.

We now turn to the construction of free deflational models. As one might anticipate from the preceding development, the free models are given by quotienting the types, terms and 2-terms by the structural equations, and any free deflational model restricts to a free opfibrational model and a free fibrational model.

Definition 6.17

(Total category generated by a deflational theory)
.

Let
\mathcal{T}=(\mathcal{L},E^{0},E^{1},\eta,E^{2})
be a deflational theory. The
deflational total category

T_{\mathsf{defl}}(\mathcal{T})
generated by
\mathcal{T}
has the equivalence classes of types
\texttt{Type}_{\mathcal{L}}
under the type congruence generated by
E^{0}\cup S^{0}
as the 0-cells, the equivalence classes of terms
\texttt{Term}^{1}_{\mathcal{L}}
under the term congruence
E^{1}\cup S_{\mathsf{defl}}^{1}
as the 1-cells, and the equivalence classes of terms
\texttt{Term}^{2}_{\mathcal{L}}
generated by
\eta\sqcup\eta_{\mathsf{str}}
under the term congruence
E^{2}\cup S_{\mathsf{defl}}^{2}
as the 2-cells.

Definition 6.18

(Zigzag base category generated by a layered signature)
.

Let
\mathcal{L}=(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathcal{M}_{\omega})
be a layered signature. The
zigzag base category

\mathsf{Zg}(B(\mathcal{L}))
generated by
\mathcal{L}
is the zigzag 2-category of the free category with indexed monoids generated by
(\Omega,\mathcal{F})
viewed as a monoidal signature.

Given a deflational theory
\mathcal{T}=(\mathcal{L},E^{0},E^{1},\eta,E^{2})
with
\mathcal{L}=(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathcal{M}_{\omega})
, define the functor
p_{\mathcal{T}}:T_{\mathsf{defl}}(\mathcal{T})\rightarrow\mathsf{Zg}(B(\mathcal{L}))
on objects by letting
A:\omega\mapsto\omega
on internal types, and on all types by extension to monoidal products. On morphisms,
p
is defined by mapping the basic, symmetry and opfibrational terms exactly as in the opfibrational case (see page
6.1
), while each fibrational term is mapped to the dual of the image of the corresponding fibrational term. Explicitly, we define:

The definition of the retrofunctors

\left(p_{\mathcal{T}},\varphi_{T,S}\right):T_{\mathsf{defl}}(\mathcal{T})(T\mid S)\rightarrow\mathsf{Zg}(B(\mathcal{L}))(pT,pS)

is more interesting. First, for every
f\in\mathcal{F}(\omega,\tau)
define the functions

\displaystyle\varphi_{A:\omega,B:\omega}(-,\eta_{f}):T_{\mathsf{defl}}(\mathcal{T})_{\omega}(A:\omega\mid B:\omega)_{0}

\displaystyle\rightarrow T_{\mathsf{defl}}(\mathcal{T})(A:\omega\mid B:\omega)_{1}

\displaystyle\varphi_{C:\tau,D:\tau}(-,\varepsilon_{f}):T_{\mathsf{defl}}(\mathcal{T})_{\bar{f};f}(C:\tau\mid D:\tau)_{0}

\displaystyle\rightarrow T_{\mathsf{defl}}(\mathcal{T})(C:\tau\mid D:\tau)_{1}

via the following assignments:

where
x:(A:\omega\mid B:\omega)
is any term in the fibre above
\omega
, while
y:(C:\tau\mid f(A):\tau)
and
z:(f(A):\tau\mid D)
are any terms in the fibre above
\tau
: note that the terms in the fibres are precisely the internal terms. Further, note that the structural equations guarantee that it does not matter which side of the term
x
the unit is applied at: the resulting 2-cells are equal. When defining the retrofunctor on the counit, note that indeed any term above
\bar{f};f
decomposes in the displayed way, by pushing any internal terms between
\vartriangleright_{f}
and
\blacktriangleleft_{f}
outside: the structural equations guarantee that it does not matter which side the terms are pushed to. The functions
\varphi_{T,S}
are defined analogously on any opfibrational-fibrational term pair. Since the only non-trivial 2-cells in
\mathsf{Zg}(B(\mathcal{L}))
are the units and the counits, it remains to extend the functions to composite terms, which is done by the following recursion:

\displaystyle\varphi_{(T,T^{\prime}),(S,S^{\prime})}\left(x\otimes y,\eta_{f\times g}\right)

\displaystyle\coloneq\varphi_{T,S}\left(x,\eta_{f}\right)\otimes\varphi_{T^{\prime},S^{\prime}}\left(y,\eta_{g}\right)

\displaystyle\varphi_{(T,T^{\prime}),(S,S^{\prime})}\left(x\otimes y,\varepsilon_{f\times g}\right)

\displaystyle\coloneq\varphi_{T,S}\left(x,\varepsilon_{f}\right)\otimes\varphi_{T^{\prime},S^{\prime}}\left(y,\varepsilon_{g}\right)

\displaystyle\varphi_{T,S}(x,\alpha;\alpha^{\prime})

\displaystyle\coloneq\varphi_{T,S}(x,\alpha);\varphi_{T,S}(y,\alpha^{\prime})

\displaystyle\varphi_{T,S}(x;y,\alpha*\alpha^{\prime})

\displaystyle\coloneq\varphi_{T,U}(x,\alpha)*\varphi_{U,S}(y,\alpha^{\prime}).

Remark 6.19
.

Note that it would have been sufficient to only define
\varphi_{A:\omega,A:\omega}\left(\mathsf{id}_{A},\eta_{f}\right)
on all the internal identity terms and, likewise,
\varphi_{f(A):\tau,f(A):\tau}\left(\vartriangleright_{f};\blacktriangleleft_{f},\varepsilon_{f}\right)
on only the opfibrational-fibrational composites – the above recursion then takes care of all the other terms. However, we find it more intuitive to define the whole function for a fixed (co)unit at once. This also makes it evident that the construction is well-defined with respect to the structural identities.

Proposition 6.20
.

For any deflational theory
\mathcal{T}
with the layered signature
\mathcal{L}
, the local retrofunctor

\left(p_{\mathcal{T}},\varphi\right):T_{\mathsf{defl}}(\mathcal{T})\rightarrow\mathsf{Zg}(B(\mathcal{L}))

is a split monoidal deflation.

Proof.

The functor
p
is a decomposition lifting by construction: given a decomposition in the base category, its chosen lifting is given by the corresponding sequence of (op)fibrational terms (i.e. by “inflating” the diagrams), interspersed with the internal terms present in the original morphism. Any two such liftings are equal, since the internal terms slide inside the diagrams. Since the codomain of
\varphi_{S,S}\left(\bar{F};F,\varepsilon_{f}\right)
, where
F:T\rightarrow S
is a lifting of
f
(i.e. some composite of opfibrational terms), is
\mathsf{id}_{S}
by definition, we indeed have a split deflation.

To show that the deflation is monoidal, we use Lemma
5.13
: it is equivalent to show that the opfibrational restriction has indexed monoids. We observe that the opfibrational restriction gives the syntactic opfibrational model
p_{\mathcal{T}}:T(\mathcal{T})\rightarrow B(\mathcal{L})
, which, by Proposition
6.8
has indexed monoids.
∎

Corollary 6.21
.

Any deflational theory
\mathcal{T}=(\mathcal{L},E^{0},E^{1},\eta,E^{2})
gives rise to the deflational model
\left(p_{\mathcal{T}},\varphi,i\right)
whose interpretation functions
i
are given by:

\displaystyle i(\omega)

\displaystyle=\omega,

\displaystyle i_{\omega,\tau}(f)

\displaystyle=f,

\displaystyle i^{\omega}(a)

\displaystyle=a:\omega,

\displaystyle i^{\omega}_{A,B}(\sigma)

\displaystyle=\sigma:(A:\omega\mid B:\omega),

\displaystyle i_{x,y}(\alpha)

\displaystyle=\alpha.

As for opfibrational theories, the syntactic models give the left adjoint to the forgetful functors from models to theories.

Theorem 6.22
.

The construction of deflational models from deflational theories extends to a functor
\mathbf{DeflTh}\rightarrow\mathbf{DeflThMod}
, which is moreover the left adjoint to the forgetful functor.

Proof.

Any morphism of deflational theories
F:\mathcal{T}\rightarrow\mathcal{K}
recursively extends to types, terms and 2-terms, as shown in Section
3
, giving the 2-functor between the total categories
T_{\mathsf{defl}}(\mathcal{T})\rightarrow T_{\mathsf{defl}}(\mathcal{K})
. The induced functor between the base categories
\mathsf{Zg}(B(\mathcal{T}))\rightarrow\mathsf{Zg}(B(\mathcal{K}))
is given by extending the action of
F
on the layers and the generators to a morphism of indexed monoids, and then further extending to a morphism of zigzag 2-categories. This gives a morphism of deflations compatible with the morphism of theories, and hence a morphism in
\mathbf{DeflThMod}
.

By Proposition
6.14
, the syntactic model of
\mathcal{T}
is the initial object of the fibre
\mathbf{OpFThMod}(\mathcal{T})
. Moreover, any morphism out of the term model of
\mathcal{T}
into any model of
\mathcal{K}
factors through the term model of
\mathcal{K}
, thus exhibiting the desired adjunction.
∎

Corollary 6.23
.

For any deflational theory
\mathcal{T}
and layered signature
\mathcal{L}
, we have the following equivalences:

\displaystyle\mathbf{DeflThMod}(\mathcal{T})

\displaystyle\simeq\left.\raisebox{1.02228pt}{$F(\mathcal{T})$}\middle/\raisebox{-1.02228pt}{$\mathbf{MonDefl}_{\mathsf{sp}}$}\right.,

\displaystyle\mathbf{DeflMod}(\mathcal{L})

\displaystyle\simeq\left.\raisebox{1.02228pt}{$F(\mathcal{L})$}\middle/\raisebox{-1.02228pt}{$\mathbf{MonDefl}_{\mathsf{sp}}$}\right..
